title: Relational Algebra Operations and Codd's Completeness
subject: Database Systems
statement: Relational algebra is a procedural query language built from selection, projection, join, union, difference, and renaming over relations. Codd's original operator set is relationally complete: it expresses every domain-independent first-order query over relations.
short: A small set of relation operators is expressive enough for every first-order database query.
detail: Selection filters rows, projection drops columns, and natural join combines relations on shared attribute names; set operations require union-compatible relations. Relational completeness is the standard benchmark for judging a query language's expressive power.
proof: Selection and projection implement conjunction and existential quantification of first-order formulas, while union, difference, and join implement disjunction, negation, and combination across relations; the standard translation between algebra and safe relational calculus gives completeness.
consequence: The core of SQL is relationally complete, while aggregation and recursion go beyond first-order expressiveness.

title: Tuple Relational Calculus and Domain Independence
subject: Database Systems
statement: Tuple relational calculus describes a query result as the set of tuples t for which a first-order formula F(t) holds. A query is domain independent when its answer does not change if the underlying domain is enlarged with fresh values.
short: Declarative queries are formulas over tuple variables, but only domain-independent formulas behave like real database queries.
detail: Syntactic safety is a decidable sufficient condition for domain independence: every quantified variable must draw values from the active domain or query constants. Full domain independence is undecidable, so practical query languages enforce syntactic restrictions.
proof: If a variable is unconstrained, enlarging the domain admits tuples with new values that were not previously answers; binding every variable to database values or constants prevents such spurious answers.
consequence: Safety rules explain why SQL cannot express certain first-order formulas and guide the translation from calculus to algebra.

title: Armstrong's Axioms for Functional Dependencies
subject: Database Systems
statement: Functional dependencies satisfy reflexivity, augmentation, and transitivity: if Y is a subset of X then X determines Y; if X determines Y then XZ determines YZ; and if X determines Y and Y determines Z then X determines Z.
latex: Y\subseteq X \Rightarrow X\to Y;\quad X\to Y \Rightarrow XZ\to YZ;\quad X\to Y,\ Y\to Z \Rightarrow X\to Z
short: Three simple inference rules capture everything that follows from a set of functional dependencies.
detail: The extra rules of pseudotransitivity and decomposition are derivable from the three axioms. A set of dependencies closed under the axioms is a canonical description of the schema's constraints.
proof: Soundness follows directly from the definition of functional dependence; completeness follows by constructing, for any dependency not derivable from F, a relation instance satisfying F but violating that dependency.
consequence: Normal-form definitions and decomposition algorithms rest on this complete inference system.

title: Attribute Closure Algorithm for Functional Dependencies
subject: Database Systems
statement: The closure X+ of an attribute set X under dependencies F is the largest set of attributes determined by X. Repeatedly add Y whenever a dependency X' to Y has its left side X' contained in the current closure; X determines Y exactly when Y belongs to X+.
short: Repeatedly applying dependencies whose left side is already known computes every attribute determined by X.
detail: The algorithm terminates after at most as many iterations as there are attributes, since each step adds at least one attribute. It also tests whether X is a superkey by checking whether the closure includes every attribute.
proof: Every addition is justified by a dependency in F, so the result is contained in the true closure; the process reaches a fixed point, so no further dependency can add an attribute, making the result the full closure.
consequence: Closure computation underlies key discovery, lossless-join testing, and normal-form checking.

title: Lossless-Join Decomposition Test
subject: Database Systems
statement: A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless with respect to dependencies F exactly when F implies that the intersection of R1 and R2 functionally determines R1 or determines R2.
latex: R_1\bowtie R_2=R \iff (R_1\cap R_2)\to R_1 \in F^{+}\ \text{or}\ (R_1\cap R_2)\to R_2 \in F^{+}
short: A two-way decomposition loses no information precisely when the shared attributes determine one of the two pieces.
detail: The chase algorithm tests the criterion by building a canonical tuple set and checking whether joining the projections can create spurious tuples. Losslessness guarantees that every tuple obtainable by rejoining was present in the original relation.
proof: If the intersection determines one side, equal shared values force equal full tuples, so the join produces no spurious rows; conversely the chase produces a counterexample relation when neither dependency holds.
consequence: Normalisation algorithms use this test to ensure schema refinement preserves all original information.

title: Dependency Preservation in Schema Decomposition
subject: Database Systems
statement: A decomposition preserves dependencies when the union of the projections of F onto each subrelation logically implies F. Without this property, enforcing a constraint requires joining the subrelations, which can be expensive.
short: Preserving dependencies lets the database check constraints locally instead of reassembling whole tuples.
detail: Third normal form always admits a dependency-preserving lossless decomposition, whereas Boyce–Codd normal form does not always do so. Designers therefore sometimes accept the weaker normal form for practical constraint enforcement.
proof: Project each dependency onto the attributes of a subrelation by computing closures within that subrelation; if the combined projected set entails the original dependencies by Armstrong's axioms, all checks can be performed locally.
consequence: The trade-off between BCNF purity and efficient constraint checking shapes real relational schemas.

title: Third Normal Form Eliminates Transitive Dependencies
subject: Database Systems
statement: A schema is in third normal form when for every nontrivial dependency X to A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute belonging to some candidate key. This excludes transitive dependencies of non-key attributes on other non-key attributes.
latex: X\to A,\ A\notin X \Rightarrow X\ \text{superkey}\ \lor\ A\ \text{prime}
short: 3NF forbids non-key facts that depend on other non-key facts rather than on the whole key.
detail: A classic violation is a relation with attributes for employee, department, and department budget: budget depends on department, which depends on employee. Splitting department information into its own relation removes the redundancy.
proof: If the condition fails, a non-key attribute is determined by a set that is not a key, giving exactly the transitive redundancy the normal form forbids; the definition is the absence of such dependencies.
consequence: 3NF reduces update anomalies while always permitting a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition.

title: Boyce-Codd Normal Form Defined
subject: Database Systems
statement: A schema is in Boyce–Codd normal form when every nontrivial functional dependency has a superkey as its determinant. It is strictly stronger than third normal form because it removes the exception for prime right-hand sides.
latex: X\to A,\ A\notin X \Rightarrow X\ \text{is a superkey}
short: BCNF requires every determinant to be a key, eliminating all redundancy due to functional dependencies.
detail: Overlapping candidate keys can leave a schema in 3NF but not BCNF, since a determinant may consist of part of a key. Decomposing to BCNF can, in rare cases, prevent dependency preservation.
proof: Replacing the 'A is prime' escape clause of 3NF with the requirement that X be a superkey yields BCNF, and schemas satisfying BCNF automatically satisfy 3NF.
consequence: BCNF gives the cleanest relational designs, at the possible cost of more joins or costlier constraint checks.

title: Multivalued Dependencies and Fourth Normal Form
subject: Database Systems
statement: A multivalued dependency X determines Y independently when the set of Y values associated with an X value does not depend on the remaining attributes. A schema is in fourth normal form when every nontrivial multivalued dependency has a superkey on its left side.
short: 4NF removes redundancy caused by two independent repeating groups in the same relation.
detail: If a person has several skills and several languages, storing every skill-language pair repeats both facts. Fourth normal form splits the relation into one relation for skills and one for languages.
proof: A multivalued dependency permits a lossless decomposition into projections on XY and on the complement; requiring the determinant to be a key ensures such independence only arises from key structure.
consequence: 4NF handles redundancy that functional dependencies alone cannot detect.

title: Join Dependencies and Fifth Normal Form
subject: Database Systems
statement: A join dependency asserts that a relation equals the natural join of projections onto several attribute subsets. Fifth normal form requires every nontrivial join dependency to be implied by the candidate keys.
short: 5NF eliminates redundancy that only appears when three or more projections are rejoined.
detail: The classic supplier-part-project example cannot be decomposed into two relations without loss but can be decomposed into three; 5NF rules out such cases unless the decomposition follows from keys.
proof: If a join dependency is not implied by keys, the relation contains combinations that are reconstructible from smaller projections, so projection and rejoin removes redundancy; 5NF forbids exactly those dependencies.
consequence: 5NF is the end point of normalisation based on join dependencies and is rarely deliberately violated.

title: ACID Properties of Transactions
subject: Database Systems
statement: ACID transactions guarantee atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability: a transaction either takes effect entirely or not at all, preserves database invariants, executes as if alone, and its committed effects survive failures.
short: ACID is the standard contract that makes database updates reliable under concurrency and crashes.
detail: Logging and recovery provide atomicity and durability, concurrency control provides isolation, and integrity constraints provide consistency. Real systems relax individual properties for performance in specific workloads.
proof: The four properties are enforced by distinct mechanisms: transaction logs for all-or-nothing commit and crash survival, locks or multiversion schemes for isolation, and constraint checks at commit for consistency.
consequence: ACID semantics let application developers reason about updates as single indivisible events.

title: Write-Ahead Logging Guarantees Atomicity
subject: Database Systems
statement: Write-ahead logging requires that the log record describing a change reach stable storage before the corresponding data page is written to disk. Recovery then replays or undoes logged actions after a crash.
short: Persisting the log first ensures recovery always knows about changes that reached disk.
detail: Log-sequence numbers order log records and page writes so recovery can determine which actions must be redone. Without the write-ahead rule, a modified page could exist on disk with no way to undo it.
proof: If a data page were written before its log record, a crash in between would leave an irrecoverable change; forcing the log record to stable storage first makes the log a complete record of every disk change.
consequence: The write-ahead rule is the foundation of almost all commercial crash-recovery schemes.

title: ARIES Recovery and Repeating History
subject: Database Systems
statement: ARIES recovery repeats history in the redo pass, replaying all logged actions including those of transactions that later abort, and then undoes only transactions active at the crash. Compensation log records make undo progress restartable.
short: ARIES first reconstructs the exact state at the crash, then rolls back only the losers.
detail: The analysis pass identifies dirty pages and active transactions from the log, redo restores the state to the crash point, and undo follows the log chain backwards for loser transactions.
proof: Redo of every action restores the database to its crash-time state; undo then writes a compensation record for each reversed action, and because those records are never undone, repeated crashes cannot repeat undo work.
consequence: Repeating history simplifies recovery and supports fine-grained locking and partial rollbacks.

title: Isolation Levels and Read Anomalies
subject: Database Systems
statement: SQL isolation levels trade concurrency against anomalies: read uncommitted allows dirty reads, read committed prevents them, repeatable read also prevents non-repeatable reads, and serializable prevents the standard anomalies.
short: Stronger isolation levels forbid more read anomalies but reduce potential concurrency.
detail: A dirty read sees uncommitted data, a non-repeatable read sees changed values on re-reading a row, and a phantom sees new rows matching a repeated predicate. Each level is defined by which of these phenomena are forbidden.
proof: The levels form a hierarchy because each additional forbidden phenomenon is a specific dependency pattern; preventing a strictly larger set of patterns can only reduce the set of admissible schedules.
consequence: Choosing an isolation level is an explicit performance-versus-correctness decision in application design.

title: Conflict Serializability and Precedence Graphs
subject: Database Systems
statement: A schedule is conflict serializable when non-conflicting operations can be commuted to produce a serial schedule. Its precedence graph, with an edge from Ti to Tj whenever Ti reads or writes an item before Tj writes it, is acyclic exactly in that case.
latex: T_i\to T_j \iff op_i(x)\prec op_j(x),\ \text{one operation writes}
short: Acyclic precedence graphs characterise schedules equivalent to some serial execution.
detail: Conflicting operations are those on the same item where at least one is a write. Topologically sorting an acyclic precedence graph gives a serial order equivalent to the original schedule.
proof: Edges record orderings of operations that cannot be swapped; a cycle means the conflicting orderings cannot all be honoured in a serial order, while a topological order of an acyclic graph yields an equivalent serial schedule.
consequence: Conflict serializability is the tractable correctness criterion used by most locking-based systems.

title: Two-Phase Locking Implies Serializability
subject: Database Systems
statement: Two-phase locking requires every transaction to acquire all its locks before releasing any. Every complete schedule produced under two-phase locking is conflict serializable.
latex: growing\ phase \to lock\ point \to shrinking\ phase
short: Forbidding new locks after the first unlock guarantees serialisable execution.
detail: The moment a transaction releases its last lock is its lock point. Ordering transactions by lock point gives a serial order consistent with the precedence graph, so no cycle can exist.
proof: If Ti has a precedence edge to Tj, Ti must have accessed a shared item before Tj, so Ti reaches its lock point no later than Tj; this makes lock points a topological order of the precedence graph.
consequence: Two-phase locking is the workhorse correctness protocol of transactional databases.

title: Strict Two-Phase Locking Prevents Cascading Aborts
subject: Database Systems
statement: Strict two-phase locking holds all exclusive locks until the transaction commits or aborts. It yields conflict-serializable schedules and prevents cascading aborts because no transaction can read data later rolled back.
short: Keeping exclusive locks to commit time avoids reads of uncommitted data that would need undoing.
detail: Rigorous two-phase locking holds both shared and exclusive locks until commit, giving an even simpler serialisation order. Strictness simplifies recovery but lowers concurrency.
proof: An exclusive lock remains held until the holder ends, so no other transaction can read or write the item in the interim; an abort therefore cannot invalidate any other transaction's reads.
consequence: Most commercial databases use a strict or rigorous locking variant for recoverability.

title: Phantom Reads and Predicate Locking
subject: Database Systems
statement: A phantom read occurs when a transaction repeats a predicate query and sees rows inserted by another transaction. Row-level locks do not cover nonexistent rows, so predicate locks or next-key locks are required to prevent phantoms.
short: New rows matching a predicate can appear even when every existing row is locked.
detail: Next-key locking combines a record lock with a gap lock on the index interval preceding the record, preventing insertions into the queried range.
proof: Locking existing rows leaves gaps between them where another transaction may insert a matching row; a lock on the predicate or the index gap closes those gaps.
consequence: Phantom handling is a major difference between repeatable-read and serializable isolation levels.

title: Snapshot Isolation and Write Skew Anomaly
subject: Database Systems
statement: Snapshot isolation lets each transaction read from a consistent snapshot but permits write skew: two concurrent transactions read overlapping data and write disjoint items, yielding a state no serial execution could produce.
short: Both transactions can commit under snapshot isolation even though together they break an invariant.
detail: In the classic example two doctors read that at least one is on call and each takes themselves off call; each writes a different row, so the first-committer-wins rule does not stop either.
proof: Each transaction sees the other's write as absent from its snapshot, and because they write disjoint items neither is aborted by the write-conflict rule; the resulting state violates the read invariant.
consequence: Snapshot isolation is not serializable, a subtlety that matters for invariant-preserving application code.

title: Optimistic Concurrency Control Validation Phase
subject: Database Systems
statement: Optimistic concurrency control lets transactions work on private copies and validates them at commit. A transaction aborts if another transaction committed a write to an item in its read set since its snapshot.
short: Assume conflicts are rare, then check at commit that the snapshot is still current.
detail: The typical phases are read, validation, and write. Backward validation checks against transactions that committed earlier; forward validation checks against currently active ones.
proof: If no committed transaction changed any item read by T after T's snapshot, T's effects can be placed immediately after that snapshot in a serial order, so cycles among committed transactions are impossible.
consequence: Optimistic control excels in read-heavy workloads where aborting the rare conflicting transaction is cheaper than locking.

title: B+ Tree Structure and Fanout
subject: Database Systems
statement: A B+ tree stores keys only in linked leaves, while internal pages hold separator keys and child pointers. Large fanout keeps a database index shallow, typically three or four disk pages deep even for millions of keys.
short: High branching keeps index traversal to a handful of disk page reads.
detail: Every leaf is at the same depth, and sibling links make range scans sequential. Internal nodes are packed with as many separators as fit in a page.
proof: Each internal page with f children multiplies the number of reachable leaves by f, so leaf count grows exponentially in height and height is logarithmic in key count.
consequence: B+ trees are the default index structure for relational databases and many file systems.

title: Clustered versus Unclustered Indexes
subject: Database Systems
statement: A clustered index determines the physical order of table rows, whereas an unclustered index stores key values together with pointers to rows. A table can have at most one clustered index but many unclustered ones.
short: Only one ordering of the rows can be physical; other orderings must be separate lookup structures.
detail: Clustered indexes make range scans of the key efficient because matching rows lie near one another. Unclustered indexes add an extra random read per matched row unless they cover the query.
proof: Rows occupy one physical sequence, so only one index can define that sequence; any other index must store a mapping from key to physical row location.
consequence: Choosing the clustered key is a high-impact physical design decision.

title: Hash Indexes for Equality Predicates
subject: Database Systems
statement: A hash index maps a key through a hash function to a bucket of row pointers. It answers equality predicates in expected constant time but cannot support ordered range scans.
short: Hashing gives fast exact-match lookups but loses key order.
detail: Overflow buckets handle collisions, and dynamic hashing schemes grow the bucket array while relocating only part of the entries. Ordered indexes are required for inequalities and prefix searches.
proof: The hash function distributes equal keys to the same bucket, so lookup examines one bucket; hashing destroys ordering information, so a range query has no way to restrict the search to a contiguous part of the index.
consequence: Workloads dominated by point lookups benefit from hash indexes; range-heavy workloads need ordered indexes.

title: Covering Index Avoids Base Table Lookups
subject: Database Systems
statement: A covering index contains every column a query needs, allowing the engine to answer the query from the index alone without fetching base table rows.
short: If the index already holds the answer, the table never has to be touched.
detail: Adding trailing columns to an index can make a query covering, but increases index size, memory use, and update cost.
proof: Index entries store values for their key columns and included columns, so when all referenced columns are present there is no need to follow a row pointer.
consequence: Covering indexes can turn a random-I/O-heavy query into a sequential index scan.

title: Selectivity Estimate Drives Index Usage
subject: Database Systems
statement: Selectivity is the fraction of rows returned by a predicate. An index is attractive when the predicate is selective enough that index probes plus row fetches cost less than a sequential scan of the whole table.
short: Few matching rows favour an index; many matching rows favour a full scan.
detail: A low-selectivity predicate, such as one matching one percent of rows, usually merits an index. A predicate matching most rows is cheaper to serve by scanning once.
proof: A full scan costs proportional to the table's page count, whereas an indexed access costs roughly the index descent plus one fetch per matching row; comparing the two gives a selectivity crossover point.
consequence: Statistics and histograms are critical because a bad selectivity estimate can produce a disastrous plan choice.

title: Database Cost-Based Query Optimizer
subject: Database Systems
statement: A cost-based query optimizer enumerates alternative logical and physical plans, estimates each plan's cost using catalog statistics, and chooses the plan with the lowest estimated cost.
short: The optimizer searches the space of equivalent plans and picks the cheapest estimated one.
detail: Transformations such as selection pushdown and join reordering generate candidates; costs combine CPU, I/O, and memory estimates from statistics such as row counts and histograms.
proof: The optimizer applies sound equivalence rules to produce plans that all compute Q, then evaluates a cost formula on each and selects the minimum, so the choice is optimal with respect to its model.
consequence: Plan quality depends on both the search space and the accuracy of the underlying statistics.

title: Selection Pushdown in Query Plans
subject: Database Systems
statement: Selection pushdown moves filters as close to the base relations as possible so that fewer rows participate in later joins and aggregations.
short: Filter early so downstream operators process fewer tuples.
detail: A filter can be pushed below a join if all attributes it references come from one side; otherwise it stays above or is split into separate filters.
proof: When p only mentions attributes of R, any joined tuple satisfying p has an R component satisfying p, and conversely every join built from filtered R tuples satisfies p, so the two plans are equivalent.
consequence: Pushdown is one of the most effective and cheapest query rewrites available to an optimizer.

title: Join Algorithms for Relational Queries
subject: Database Systems
statement: Nested-loop join compares pairs of rows, hash join builds a hash table on one input and probes with the other, and sort-merge join sorts both inputs and merges on the join key. Hash join is usually preferred for large equi-joins, sort-merge when inputs are already ordered.
short: Three classic strategies trade memory, sorting cost, and comparison count.
detail: Block nested loops reduce I/O by buffering pages of the outer relation. Grace hash join partitions overflow to disk when the build side exceeds memory.
proof: Nested loops examines every pair, hash join restricts comparisons to rows sharing a hash bucket, and sort-merge advances two cursors in sorted order, visiting each input once after sorting.
consequence: The choice of join algorithm dominates the cost of analytical queries over large tables.

title: Dynamic Programming for Join Order Selection
subject: Database Systems
statement: Dynamic-programming join enumeration computes the cheapest plan for each subset of relations by combining optimal subplans of smaller subsets. It is optimal for a cost model satisfying the principle of optimality but exponential in the number of relations.
short: Solve every subset once and reuse those optimal subplans to build larger ones.
detail: Systems switch to greedy or randomized search beyond roughly ten relations because the subset count grows as two to the number of relations.
proof: An optimal plan for S splits into two subplans whose own replacements by cheaper equivalents cannot increase total cost, so combining optimal subplans over all splits finds the minimum.
consequence: This algorithm explains why optimizer quality matters most for queries joining many tables.

title: Materialized Views and Query Rewriting
subject: Database Systems
statement: A materialized view stores a query result physically, replacing repeated expensive computation with reads. Optimizers can rewrite matching queries to use the stored result, provided freshness requirements are met.
short: Cache a derived table and let the optimizer redirect compatible queries to it.
detail: Refresh strategies range from immediate maintenance on every base update to periodic rebuilding. Query rewriting must account for nulls, duplicates, and aggregate semantics.
proof: If the view definition is algebraically equivalent to a subexpression of the query, substituting the stored result preserves the answer under the same relational semantics.
consequence: Materialized views are a key performance tool in data warehouses with repetitive aggregate queries.

title: Consistent Hashing for Data Sharding
subject: Database Systems
statement: Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a circular identifier space and assigns each key to the first node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only keys in the affected arc.
short: Only a small fraction of keys change owners when the cluster size changes.
detail: Virtual nodes, multiple points per physical node, smooth the load distribution and reduce hotspots. The expected fraction of remapped keys when adding one node among n is about one over n.
proof: Keys between a newly inserted node and its predecessor are the only ones whose clockwise successor changes, so the shared arc length determines the remapped fraction.
consequence: Consistent hashing keeps rebalancing cost low in distributed key-value stores and sharded databases.

title: Multiversion Concurrency Control Snapshot Reads
subject: Database Systems
statement: Multiversion concurrency control retains old versions of rows tagged with transaction timestamps. A transaction reads the version visible at its snapshot, so readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers.
short: Keeping old versions lets each reader see a stable past state without locking.
detail: Version chains are garbage-collected once no active snapshot needs them. MVCC combines well with optimistic or first-committer-wins conflict rules.
proof: Visibility rules choose the newest version whose creator committed before the reader's snapshot and whose deleter committed after it, giving every reader a consistent point-in-time view.
consequence: MVCC underlies high-concurrency systems such as PostgreSQL and snapshot-isolation engines.

title: Bitmap Indexes for Low-Cardinality Columns
subject: Database Systems
statement: A bitmap index stores one bit per row for each distinct value of a low-cardinality column. Bitwise AND and OR implement conjunctions and disjunctions of predicates with great speed, but updates are costly.
short: Bit vectors turn set operations on rows into cheap bit-parallel operations.
detail: Compressed bitmaps such as Roaring bitmaps reduce storage for sparse or clustered values. Columns with very high cardinality produce too many bitmaps to be practical.
proof: Each bit vector marks exactly the rows having a value, and a bitwise AND or OR computes the intersection or union of those row sets in one pass over machine words.
consequence: Bitmap indexes are especially effective in read-mostly data warehouses with many low-cardinality dimensions.

title: Candidate Key Discovery from Functional Dependencies
subject: Database Systems
statement: A candidate key is a minimal attribute set whose closure includes every attribute. Enumerating subsets in order of increasing size and testing each closure finds all candidate keys.
short: Find the smallest attribute sets that determine the entire relation.
detail: Attributes that appear only on right-hand sides of dependencies cannot belong to any key, which prunes the search. Attributes that appear on neither side must belong to every key.
proof: Any superset of a key is a superkey by augmentation, so the first subsets whose closure covers all attributes are exactly the minimal ones, i.e. the candidate keys.
consequence: Key discovery is the first step in normal-form analysis and decomposition design.

title: Process Control Block and Context Switch
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A process control block is the kernel structure holding a process's state, program counter, registers, memory map, open files, and scheduling data. A context switch saves the outgoing process's state there and loads the incoming process's state.
short: The kernel stores each process's execution context so it can be paused and resumed.
detail: Context switches are triggered by timer interrupts, system calls, or blocking operations. Their cost motivates schedulers to avoid switching too frequently.
proof: Before selecting another process, the kernel saves registers and status into the outgoing PCB; restoring the incoming PCB's registers makes that process continue exactly where it stopped.
consequence: PCBs make multiprogramming possible and underpin process isolation and scheduling.

title: CPU Scheduling Metrics and Trade-offs
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Turnaround time is completion minus arrival, waiting time is total time in the ready queue, response time is first response minus arrival, and throughput is completed jobs per unit time. Scheduling policies trade these metrics against one another.
short: Different scheduling goals favour different definitions of speed and fairness.
detail: Interactive systems prioritise low response time and jitter, while batch systems may prioritise throughput or mean turnaround. No single policy optimises all metrics simultaneously.
proof: These quantities are derived by decomposing a job's residency into arrival-to-start, start-to-finish, and I/O intervals, giving the stated equalities.
consequence: Explicit metric choices are necessary before comparing scheduling algorithms.

title: Convoy Effect in First-Come First-Served Scheduling
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Under first-come first-served scheduling, many short jobs queue behind one long CPU-bound job, forming a convoy of processes waiting for a single long burst. Mean waiting time can become very large.
short: One long nonpreemptive job can delay an entire queue of short jobs.
detail: The effect is particularly harmful when short jobs would have finished quickly and released resources. Preemptive policies such as round robin mitigate it.
proof: Each short job arriving behind the long job waits for the entire remaining burst, and the waiting times accumulate linearly with the number of queued jobs.
consequence: FIFO fairness does not imply good average performance, motivating more sophisticated schedulers.

title: Shortest Job First Minimises Mean Waiting Time
subject: Operating Systems
statement: For a batch of jobs available simultaneously, shortest-job-first scheduling minimises the mean waiting time and is optimal among nonpreemptive policies for that metric.
short: Running the shortest job next removes the largest possible contribution to total waiting.
detail: The preemptive variant, shortest remaining time first, is optimal when jobs arrive over time and preemption is free. Both require estimates or knowledge of burst lengths.
proof: Swapping an adjacent pair with the longer job first reduces total waiting by the difference of their bursts, so repeatedly sorting by increasing burst length eliminates all such improvements and achieves the minimum.
consequence: This optimality result is the theoretical benchmark against which practical schedulers are compared.

title: Round-Robin Scheduling and Time Quantum
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Round-robin scheduling gives each ready process a fixed time quantum and cycles through the ready queue. A process that does not finish within its quantum is placed at the back of the queue.
short: A fixed quantum bounds how long any ready process waits for its next turn.
detail: A very large quantum degenerates toward first-come first-served, while a very small one causes excessive context-switch overhead.
proof: With n ready processes and quantum q, at most n-1 other processes run before the same process is scheduled again, giving the stated bound on response delay.
consequence: Round robin provides good interactive response and is the basis of many time-sharing schedulers.

title: Starvation under Priority Scheduling
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes when higher-priority work arrives continuously. Aging gradually raises the effective priority of waiting processes to bound their delay.
short: Without aging, a busy high-priority queue can postpone low-priority work indefinitely.
detail: Starvation differs from deadlock: the system keeps making progress, but some processes never progress. Aging converts starvation into bounded waiting.
proof: If the highest-priority queue never becomes empty, a low-priority process is never selected; increasing its priority with waiting time eventually makes it the highest-priority runnable process.
consequence: Starvation avoidance is a required property of any fair scheduler.

title: Multilevel Feedback Queue Scheduling
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A multilevel feedback queue uses several priority queues and moves jobs between them according to observed behaviour. Jobs that yield frequently remain high, while CPU-bound jobs drift to lower-priority queues with longer quanta.
short: Observed short bursts earn high priority without knowing job lengths in advance.
detail: Demotion happens when a job exhausts its quantum; promotion can occur after waiting or I/O. The scheme approximates shortest remaining processing time adaptively.
proof: Jobs that finish quickly or block early never get demoted, so they stay in high-priority queues and receive prompt service; long jobs settle into lower queues where fewer context switches occur.
consequence: Multilevel feedback queues were historically used in general-purpose time-sharing systems and remain a standard design pattern.

title: Belady's Anomaly for FIFO Replacement
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Belady's anomaly is the observation that FIFO page replacement can incur more page faults with more frames. Adding memory is therefore not monotonically beneficial for every replacement policy.
short: More frames can perversely cause more faults under FIFO because the evicted pages change.
detail: The classic counterexample uses three and four frames with a nine-access reference string. Stack algorithms such as LRU and OPT do not exhibit the anomaly.
proof: For a suitable reference string, the extra frame changes which page FIFO evicts, causing a frequently reused page to be absent at a crucial moment; a direct trace of the string establishes the inequality.
consequence: The anomaly motivated the theory of stack replacement algorithms, whose fault sets are nested in memory size.

title: Optimal Page Replacement Lower Bound
subject: Operating Systems
statement: OPT replaces the page whose next use is farthest in the future and achieves the minimum possible number of faults for a given reference string and frame count. It is an offline algorithm requiring knowledge of the future.
short: Evicting the page needed farthest in the future is provably best, if you know the future.
detail: OPT is used as a benchmark in simulation studies because no online policy can beat it. LRU approximates it using recent past accesses as a proxy for future ones.
proof: An exchange argument transforms any optimal policy into one that evicts the farthest-next-use page without increasing faults, so OPT's choices are optimal at every fault.
consequence: OPT provides the lower bound against which practical replacement policies are evaluated.

title: Clock Page Replacement Approximation
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The clock algorithm scans a circular list of resident pages and clears each page's use bit; the first page whose bit is already clear is evicted.
short: A circular scan with use bits approximates LRU at low cost.
detail: Variants use additional modified bits to prefer clean victims and reduce write-back cost. The hand of the clock advances only on page faults, keeping overhead small.
proof: A set use bit indicates recent access, so clearing it gives that page one more chance; a page whose bit is clear on the current sweep has not been used since the previous sweep and is a reasonable victim.
consequence: Clock and its variants are widely used because they need only a bit per page and no per-access list updates.

title: Working Set Model of Program Locality
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The working set of a process at time t is the set of pages referenced during the preceding window of length delta. The working-set model asserts that a process needs this set resident to avoid excessive paging.
short: Recently used pages form a good predictor of the pages a process needs next.
detail: The model explains why multiprogramming degree should adapt to the sum of working sets. Page-fault frequency is a practical proxy for working-set size.
proof: Temporal locality means references cluster in time, so pages seen in the recent window have a high probability of being referenced again soon.
consequence: Working-set ideas guide memory allocation and thrashing prevention in real systems.

title: Demand Paging and Page Fault Service
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Demand paging loads a page only when access to an absent page triggers a fault. The handler finds the page on disk, selects a victim if memory is full, updates the page table, and restarts the faulting instruction.
short: Pages are fetched lazily and the interrupted instruction is simply retried.
detail: Hardware sets a fault when the present bit is clear; the kernel distinguishes a legitimate page-in from an access violation by checking the process's virtual address map.
proof: Restarting the faulting instruction after installing the page makes the delay invisible to the program, which observes the same architectural state as if the page had always been resident.
consequence: Demand paging enables large virtual address spaces and efficient memory sharing.

title: Thrashing and Page Fault Frequency
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Thrashing occurs when a system spends more time handling page faults than executing useful work, usually because the sum of active working sets exceeds physical memory. Lowering multiprogramming or adding memory restores progress.
short: Too many processes competing for too few frames cause a self-sustaining storm of faults.
detail: Page-fault frequency monitors can detect thrashing: if the rate is too high, the kernel suspends a process; if too low, it can admit another.
proof: When each process lacks frames for its working set, servicing one fault evicts a page another process will soon need, so fault rates rise and useful work stalls.
consequence: Thrashing control is a classic example of feedback-based resource management.

title: Copy-on-Write Fork Implementation
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Copy-on-write fork lets parent and child initially share physical pages marked read-only. A store to a shared page traps the kernel, which creates a private copy for the writing process and resumes execution.
short: Defer copying until a process actually modifies a shared page.
detail: The technique makes process creation cheap for workloads that immediately execute a new program. Kernel bookkeeping tracks reference counts on shared page frames.
proof: Sharing costs nothing for pages neither process writes; the write fault identifies exactly which page must become private, preserving the illusion of separate address spaces.
consequence: Copy-on-write is essential for fast fork-based process creation and for memory-efficient snapshots.

title: Page Table Dirty and Referenced Bits
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A page table entry typically carries a present bit, protection bits, a referenced bit set on access, and a dirty bit set on modification. The operating system uses these bits for protection decisions and page replacement.
short: Hardware-maintained bits give the kernel cheap hints about recent page behaviour.
detail: Referenced bits support approximate LRU or clock replacement; dirty bits avoid writing clean pages back to disk when evicting.
proof: Hardware sets reference and dirty bits automatically on memory accesses, so the kernel obtains usage information without trapping on every access.
consequence: These bits are a small but crucial interface between memory management hardware and the operating system.

title: Deadlock Necessary Conditions
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption of resources, and a circular wait among processes. All four conditions must hold simultaneously.
short: Breaking any one of the four Coffman conditions prevents deadlock.
detail: Deadlock avoidance and prevention strategies each target a different condition: spooling removes mutual exclusion, atomic acquisition removes hold-and-wait, preemption removes no-preemption, and ordering removes circular wait.
proof: If any condition fails, some process can always acquire a needed resource or be forced to release one, so the system cannot remain permanently stuck.
consequence: The four conditions organise the entire taxonomy of deadlock handling techniques.

title: Resource Allocation Graph Deadlock Detection
subject: Operating Systems
statement: In a resource allocation graph with one instance per resource type, a cycle is necessary and sufficient for deadlock. With multiple instances, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.
short: Cycles signal deadlock exactly when each resource type has a single instance.
detail: Detection periodically searches for cycles and then aborts or rolls back a process in each cycle. The general multiple-instance case uses a matrix-based detection algorithm analogous to the safety test.
proof: A cycle of single-instance resources leaves every process in it waiting for a resource held by another member, so none can proceed; conversely a deadlock must contain such a cycle. With multiple instances, an available copy may break a cycle.
consequence: Graph-based detection is simple and efficient for systems with unique resources.

title: Banker's Algorithm for Deadlock Avoidance
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The banker's algorithm grants a request only if a safe sequence exists in which every remaining process can finish using currently available resources plus those released by finished processes.
short: Never let the system enter a state from which all processes might not finish.
detail: The algorithm maintains available, maximum, allocation, and need matrices. It rejects requests that would make the state unsafe even if they do not immediately deadlock.
proof: The safety test repeatedly adds the resources of a process whose remaining need fits the available pool; if all processes can be ordered this way, that order is a safe sequence.
consequence: Avoidance is safer than detection but requires advance knowledge of maximum resource needs.

title: Deadlock Prevention by Resource Ordering
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Imposing a total order on resource types and requiring processes to request resources in increasing order makes circular wait impossible.
short: A global ordering rule rules out cycles in the wait-for relation.
detail: The scheme may force a process to hold high-order resources longer than needed, reducing concurrency. Other prevention strategies attack different Coffman conditions instead.
proof: Along any chain of hold-and-wait edges resource types strictly increase, so returning to the starting process would require a strict increase that ends where it began, which is impossible.
consequence: Ordering is a practical prevention strategy when resource types are few and stable.

title: Mutex Locks and Critical Sections
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A mutex is a lock allowing only one thread at a time inside a critical section. Acquiring and releasing it enforces mutual exclusion on shared state.
short: A mutex serialises access to shared state so updates cannot interleave.
detail: Implementations rely on atomic hardware primitives such as test-and-set or compare-and-swap. Recursive mutexes allow reacquisition by the same thread, while error-checking mutexes detect misuse.
proof: The atomic lock operation ensures only one thread observes the unlocked state and enters; all others wait until the holder releases it.
consequence: Mutexes are the basic building block for thread-safe software.

title: Semaphores as Counting Synchronisation Primitives
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A semaphore is an integer counter with atomic wait and signal operations; wait blocks when the counter is zero. Counting semaphores manage several identical resources, and binary semaphores act as locks.
latex: P(s):\ s\leftarrow s-1,\quad V(s):\ s\leftarrow s+1
short: An atomic counter controls how many threads may proceed past a point.
detail: A blocked thread is placed on a queue and awakened by a later signal. Semaphores can also express ordering constraints between threads, not just mutual exclusion.
proof: Atomicity prevents two concurrent waits from both decrementing a counter of one below zero, so at most the available count of threads is admitted.
consequence: Semaphores express both mutual exclusion and resource counting in a single primitive.

title: Monitors and Condition Variables
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A monitor encapsulates shared data and procedures, allowing at most one thread to execute inside it at a time. Condition variables inside a monitor let threads wait for a state condition and be signaled when it may hold.
short: Monitors bundle locking and waiting into one structured abstraction.
detail: Calling wait atomically releases the monitor lock and blocks; signal wakes a waiting thread, which reacquires the lock before continuing. Mesa semantics allow spurious wakeups and require condition testing in a loop.
proof: Mutual exclusion at monitor entry protects the shared state, while the atomic release-and-block of wait avoids missing a signal between testing a condition and sleeping.
consequence: Monitors are the synchronisation model behind Java and many modern languages.

title: Bounded-Buffer Producer-Consumer Problem
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The bounded-buffer producer–consumer problem coordinates producers and consumers with three semaphores: one counting empty slots, one counting full slots, and one protecting the buffer.
short: Two counting semaphores bound occupancy while a mutex protects the queue.
detail: A producer waits for an empty slot, inserts an item under the mutex, and signals a full slot; a consumer performs the reverse operations.
proof: The empty count never exceeds the buffer capacity because producers decrement it before inserting, the full count prevents consumers from removing absent items, and the mutex serialises access to the shared buffer.
consequence: The pattern underlies pipelines, message queues, and bounded blocking queues.

title: Readers-Writers Problem and Writer Starvation
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The readers–writers problem permits concurrent readers but requires exclusive access for writers. A writer-preference policy blocks new readers once a writer is waiting so writers cannot starve.
latex: readers>0 \Rightarrow writers wait;\ writer\_waiting \Rightarrow new\ readers\ wait
short: Reader concurrency is valuable, but unbounded reader arrival can starve writers forever.
detail: A reader count and mutex let the first reader acquire a database lock and the last reader release it. Writer preference introduces a queue to give waiting writers priority.
proof: Without preference, a continuous stream of new readers keeps the read lock held indefinitely; blocking arrivals once a writer waits guarantees the writer eventually acquires exclusive access.
consequence: The problem illustrates how fairness, not just mutual exclusion, must be designed explicitly.

title: Dining Philosophers and Resource Hierarchy
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The dining philosophers problem illustrates deadlock when each process holds one resource while waiting for another held by a neighbour. Imposing a global order on resources, or limiting the number of concurrent diners, breaks the circular wait.
short: Symmetric hold-and-wait among neighbours deadlocks unless a rule breaks the symmetry.
detail: The resource hierarchy solution requires every philosopher to pick the lower-numbered fork first. A semaphore allowing at most n-1 philosophers also prevents deadlock.
proof: With a global order, the philosopher holding the highest-needed lower fork can always acquire the other, so at least one diner progresses and the cycle is broken.
consequence: The fable is a standard teaching example for deadlock conditions and prevention.

title: Futex Fast Path and Kernel Slow Path
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A futex performs uncontended lock operations entirely in user space with atomic instructions and enters the kernel only when a thread must block or wake another.
latex: CAS(word) \text{ fast path};\ futex(SYS) \text{ slow path}
short: Keep the common uncontended case free of system calls.
detail: The kernel futex call registers a waiter on a user-space address and supports wake operations. Shared futexes work across processes via mapped memory.
proof: Uncontended acquisition and release reduce to a compare-and-swap on a user-space word; the kernel is involved only when the atomic operation detects contention and blocking is necessary.
consequence: Futexes are the foundation of low-overhead locking in Linux thread libraries.

title: Inodes and Directory Entries
subject: Operating Systems
statement: In Unix-like file systems, an inode holds a file's metadata and data-block pointers, while directory entries map human-readable names to inode numbers.
short: Names are separate from file identity, which is stored in the inode.
detail: Hard links are additional directory entries pointing to the same inode; the file's data disappears only when the last link is removed.
proof: Separating names from metadata lets several names refer to one inode, so the kernel maintains a link count in the inode to know when to free its blocks.
consequence: The inode abstraction underpins links, permissions, and file identity in Unix systems.

title: Journaling File Systems and Write Ordering
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A journaling file system writes a record of intended metadata changes before applying them, so a crash can be repaired by replaying committed transactions and discarding incomplete ones.
short: Recording intent first turns crash recovery into log replay rather than a full scan.
detail: Ordering modes differ in whether file data is written before metadata. Full journaling of data gives the strongest guarantees at the cost of extra writes.
proof: Because the log states which operations were intended and which committed, recovery can distinguish completed transactions from partial ones and restore a consistent metadata state.
consequence: Journaling dramatically reduces file system check time after unclean shutdowns.

title: Hard Links versus Symbolic Links
subject: Operating Systems
statement: A hard link is another directory entry for an existing inode, while a symbolic link is a separate file containing a pathname to a target. Deleting the original name leaves a hard link working but breaks a symbolic link.
short: Hard links share identity; symbolic links store a redirect.
detail: Hard links generally cannot cross file system boundaries and cannot link directories. Symbolic links can cross boundaries but become dangling if the target is moved or removed.
proof: Hard links reference the inode directly, so they remain valid as long as the inode exists; symbolic links are resolved by path lookup at access time, so moving the target breaks resolution.
consequence: The distinction affects backup, deletion, and path-resolution behaviour.

title: RAID Levels and Redundancy
subject: Operating Systems
statement: RAID combines disks for throughput, capacity, or fault tolerance: RAID 0 stripes without redundancy, RAID 1 mirrors, RAID 5 stripes with distributed parity, and RAID 6 adds a second parity stripe.
short: Striping improves performance, mirroring or parity survives disk failure.
detail: Parity is computed with bitwise exclusive-or, allowing a failed disk to be reconstructed from surviving blocks and parity. RAID 6 tolerates two simultaneous failures.
proof: Exclusive-or parity satisfies data_1 xor ... xor data_k = parity, so any missing block is recovered by XORing all other blocks and the parity block.
consequence: RAID is the standard way to trade disk count for reliability and throughput.

title: Rate-Monotonic Scheduling and Priorities
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Rate-monotonic scheduling assigns fixed priorities by period, with shorter periods receiving higher priority. For independent periodic tasks whose deadlines equal their periods, it is optimal among fixed-priority policies.
short: Shorter periods earn higher fixed priority and give the best fixed-priority schedule.
detail: Feasibility is guaranteed when total utilisation is at most n times the nth root of two, though some sets above that bound are still schedulable. Exact response-time analysis gives a tighter test.
proof: An exchange argument shows that if some fixed-priority assignment is feasible, swapping adjacent priority assignments so the shorter period is higher preserves feasibility; hence rate-monotonic order is optimal.
consequence: Rate-monotonic analysis is a standard design tool for hard real-time systems.

title: Earliest Deadline First Scheduling Optimality
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Earliest-deadline-first scheduling always runs the ready task with the nearest absolute deadline. On a single processor it is optimal for independent preemptive tasks with deadlines equal to periods.
short: The most urgent task runs first, and no other policy can meet a deadline EDF misses.
detail: EDF can achieve utilisation up to one hundred percent but is less predictable under overload than fixed-priority scheduling, where low-priority tasks simply miss deadlines.
proof: If EDF misses a deadline, a feasibility argument shows every legal schedule misses one: any schedule can be transformed into an EDF schedule without increasing any job's lateness by swapping adjacent out-of-order executions.
consequence: EDF is the theoretical optimum for uniprocessor dynamic-priority real-time scheduling.

title: Priority Inversion and Priority Inheritance
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task while a medium-priority task preempts the holder. Priority inheritance temporarily raises the holder to the highest priority of waiting tasks.
short: Temporarily boost the lock holder so it can finish and release the lock.
detail: The Mars Pathfinder mission famously experienced priority inversion. Priority ceilings offer an alternative by assigning each lock a fixed high priority.
proof: Raising the holder above the medium-priority task lets it complete its critical section, after which the high-priority task proceeds, hence the inversion is bounded by one critical section.
consequence: Priority inheritance is required in real-time systems that share resources across priority levels.

title: Jitter in Real-Time Systems
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Jitter is variation in the start or completion times of periodically recurring tasks relative to an ideal schedule. Real-time systems constrain jitter because variability can violate deadlines even when average latency is low.
short: Predictable timing matters as much as fast average timing.
detail: Interrupt handling, cache misses, and garbage collection are common sources of jitter. Hard real-time systems use dedicated scheduling and minimal interrupt masking to bound it.
proof: Each invocation's actual start time differs from its ideal periodic instant by accumulated interference, so the maximum deviation quantifies timing variability.
consequence: Jitter bounds are central to audio, control loops, and networked media applications.

title: Container Namespaces and Control Groups
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Linux namespaces give a group of processes private views of resources such as process identifiers, mount points, and network interfaces. Control groups limit and account for their CPU, memory, and I/O usage.
short: Namespaces virtualise what a process sees; control groups cap what it can consume.
detail: Containers combine namespaces, cgroups, and a private filesystem image without running a separate kernel. They are lighter than virtual machines but share the host kernel.
proof: The kernel tags processes with namespace memberships so lookups resolve within their private view, while cgroup membership routes resource accounting and enforcement to the group's limits.
consequence: Namespaces and cgroups are the technical foundation of modern container runtimes.

title: DMA and Interrupt-Driven I/O
subject: Operating Systems
statement: Direct memory access lets a device transfer blocks of data between itself and main memory without the CPU copying each word. The CPU programs the controller and receives an interrupt when the transfer completes.
short: The CPU sets up the transfer and is interrupted only when it finishes.
detail: DMA reduces CPU overhead for disks, network cards, and graphics devices. The memory controller must arbitrate bus access between the CPU and the DMA engine.
proof: The controller takes over bus transactions for the duration of the transfer, so the CPU is free to run other work until the completion interrupt signals that the buffer is ready.
consequence: DMA is essential for high-throughput I/O without saturating the processor.

title: Lexical Analysis with Finite Automata
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A lexer scans characters and groups them into tokens using patterns described by regular expressions. A scanner generator compiles token patterns into a finite automaton that recognises token classes.
short: Token patterns become automata that consume input in linear time.
detail: Longest-match rules and token priorities resolve cases where several patterns match a prefix. The resulting token stream is the parser's input.
proof: Regular expressions and finite automata recognise the same language class, so converting each token pattern to an automaton and taking their union recognises exactly the token set.
consequence: Clean separation of lexing and parsing simplifies both phases of a compiler front end.

title: DFA Minimisation in Lexer Generation
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Every regular language has a unique minimal DFA up to renaming of states. Partition refinement splits blocks of states that behave differently on some input symbol until no further split is possible.
short: Merge indistinguishable automaton states to obtain the smallest scanner.
detail: The algorithm starts with accepting and non-accepting states and refines by transition behaviour. It runs in polynomial time in the number of states.
proof: States in one block are equivalent for all strings observed so far; refining on each symbol separates exactly states distinguishable by some suffix, and the final quotient is minimal and unique.
consequence: Minimisation keeps generated scanners small and fast.

title: Recursive-Descent Parsing and Backtracking
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A recursive-descent parser implements grammar productions as mutually recursive procedures that consume tokens. Predictive recursive descent requires disjoint first sets for alternatives to avoid backtracking.
short: Each grammar production becomes a procedure that recognises its right-hand side.
detail: Backtracking parsers try alternatives and restore the input position on failure. Left recursion must be eliminated before using recursive descent.
proof: Each procedure consumes the terminals of its production and calls procedures for nonterminals, so the resulting call tree mirrors a valid derivation of the input string.
consequence: LL grammars support simple, efficient, hand-written parsers.

title: LR(0) Item Sets and Shift-Reduce Parsing
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: An LR(0) item is a production with a marker showing how much of its right-hand side has been consumed. Canonical collections of item sets form the states of a shift-reduce parser operating with a stack and input lookahead.
short: Item sets track all possible production positions consistent with the prefix already parsed.
detail: Shift moves a terminal onto the stack; reduce replaces a production's right-hand side by its left-hand side. Conflicts signal that the grammar is not LR(0).
proof: Each item set records valid positions in productions for the parsed prefix, so shifting or reducing according to the automaton maintains a stack encoding a viable prefix.
consequence: LR parsing recognises a broad class of grammars deterministically in linear time.

title: LALR Parser Construction
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: LALR parser generation merges LR(1) item sets with identical cores while retaining lookahead information. The resulting tables are much smaller than canonical LR(1) tables and may introduce reduce-reduce conflicts.
short: Merging lookahead states trades a little power for much smaller tables.
detail: Yacc and Bison generate LALR parsers by default. Grammars that are LALR-compatible avoid the conflicts that merging can create.
proof: Merging states with the same LR(0) core unions their lookahead sets; the automaton still recognises the same viable prefixes, but extra lookaheads can create spurious conflicts.
consequence: LALR is the practical standard for parser generators.

title: Ambiguous Grammars and Operator Precedence
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: An ambiguous grammar admits more than one parse tree for a string. Parser generators usually resolve common ambiguities by declaring operator precedence and associativity instead of rewriting the grammar.
short: Precedence declarations choose one of several possible parse trees.
detail: A shift-reduce conflict on an expression grammar is resolved by comparing the precedence of the pending operator with the next token.
proof: The expression 1+2*3 has two derivations under the ambiguous grammar; precedence rules resolve the shift-reduce conflict so that multiplication binds tighter.
consequence: Ambiguity resolution directly determines the semantics of expressions.

title: Syntax Error Recovery in Parsers
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Error recovery techniques such as panic mode discard tokens until a synchronising token is found, allowing a parser to continue and report several errors in one run.
short: Skip forward to a token that can legitimately follow the faulty construct.
detail: Other strategies include phrase-level recovery and error productions. Poor recovery can cascade, producing many spurious messages after the first error.
proof: Discarding input until a token in the follow set of the current nonterminal restores a consistent parsing state, so subsequent input can be analysed.
consequence: Effective recovery greatly improves the developer experience of a compiler.

title: Concrete versus Abstract Syntax Trees
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A concrete syntax tree records every grammar symbol in a derivation, while an abstract syntax tree retains only semantically meaningful nodes. Compilers normally discard punctuation and syntactic sugar after parsing.
short: The AST is the grammar-free skeleton the rest of the compiler works with.
detail: Unary productions introduced for precedence are collapsed, and tokens such as semicolons are dropped, leaving operator and operand nodes.
proof: Removing punctuation and chain nodes preserves the semantic content of a derivation while shrinking the tree, so subsequent passes can operate on a cleaner representation.
consequence: The AST is the interface between the parser and semantic analysis.

title: Three-Address Code as an Intermediate Representation
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Three-address code is an intermediate representation in which each instruction has at most three operands and one operator, such as t1 = t2 + t3. It makes evaluation order explicit while remaining largely machine independent.
short: Flatten expressions into simple instructions with temporaries.
detail: Quadruples and triples are common implementations. Three-address code is close enough to machine code for optimisation yet far enough to stay portable.
proof: Introducing a fresh temporary for each subexpression flattens an arbitrary syntax tree into instructions each having at most three operands.
consequence: It is a widely used bridge between syntax trees and target machine code.

title: Control-Flow Graphs and Basic Blocks
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A basic block is a maximal straight-line instruction sequence with a single entry and a single exit. A control-flow graph uses basic blocks as nodes and possible control transfers as edges.
short: Partition code into straight-line chunks and connect them by branches.
detail: Leaders are the first instruction, branch targets, and instructions following branches. Loops and dominators are defined on the resulting graph.
proof: Splitting at leaders gives maximal straight-line regions, and adding an edge for every possible transfer between them yields a graph representing all execution paths.
consequence: Nearly all dataflow analyses and optimisations operate on control-flow graphs.

title: Phi Nodes in SSA Merging
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: In static single assignment form a phi node selects a value according to the control-flow edge used to reach a join point. Phi nodes give each variable exactly one definition even where paths merge.
short: A phi node chooses among reaching definitions at a merge point.
detail: Phi nodes are later lowered into moves in predecessor blocks during register allocation. Correct placement is computed from dominance frontiers.
proof: Inserting a phi whose arguments are the definitions reaching each incoming edge preserves value semantics while ensuring every variable has a single defining instruction.
consequence: SSA simplifies constant propagation, dead-code elimination, and many other passes.

title: Dominator Trees and Immediate Dominators
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Node d dominates node n in a control-flow graph if every path from the entry to n passes through d. The immediate dominator of n is its closest strict dominator, and these relations form the dominator tree.
short: Dominators identify nodes that must execute before a given point.
detail: Dominance frontiers, built from the dominator tree, determine where phi nodes are required in SSA conversion.
proof: Dominance is reflexive and transitive and each node except the entry has a unique immediate dominator, so the relation forms a tree rooted at the entry.
consequence: Dominators underpin loop detection, SSA construction, and code motion.

title: Liveness Analysis by Backward Dataflow
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A variable is live at a point if its current value may be used before being redefined. Liveness analysis propagates use and definition sets backwards over the control-flow graph to a fixed point.
short: Work backwards from uses to find variables whose values still matter.
detail: The analysis is a must-free may-analysis: a variable is live if some path from the point reaches a use before a definition.
proof: Uses make variables live at block entry unless defined first, and live variables at a successor's entry are live at the block's exit; iterating to a fixed point handles cycles in loops.
consequence: Liveness drives register allocation, dead-code elimination, and spill decisions.

title: Reaching Definitions Analysis
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Reaching definitions analysis determines which assignments may have produced the current value of a variable at each program point. It is a forward may-analysis over the control-flow graph.
short: Track which definitions can still flow to each point without being overwritten.
detail: A definition kills previous definitions of the same variable and generates itself. Join points union the incoming definition sets.
proof: A definition reaches a point exactly when a path exists from its assignment to that point with no intervening redefinition; union at joins and propagation through blocks compute those paths.
consequence: Reaching definitions support constant propagation and use-def chains.

title: Constant Folding and Propagation
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Constant folding evaluates compile-time constant expressions, and constant propagation replaces variables known to hold constants with those values. The passes are usually iterated until no further change occurs.
short: Compute what is known at compile time and reuse it everywhere.
detail: Sparse conditional constant propagation combines propagation with branch reachability to avoid incorrect substitutions on infeasible paths.
proof: Replacing a variable by a provably equal constant and evaluating pure operators preserves semantics under the language's evaluation rules.
consequence: These are among the simplest and most widely applied compiler optimisations.

title: Dead Code Elimination
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Dead code elimination removes instructions whose results are never used and that have no side effects. Liveness information identifies such instructions safely.
short: Unused pure computations can be deleted without changing behaviour.
detail: Aggressive elimination also removes unreachable basic blocks and branches with constant conditions.
proof: If the defined value is not live at the instruction's exit and the instruction has no side effects, executing it cannot influence any later observable action.
consequence: Dead-code removal shrinks binaries and reduces wasted runtime work.

title: Common Subexpression Elimination
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Common subexpression elimination replaces repeated computations of the same expression with a single previously computed value, provided no operand changed in between.
short: Reuse a result when the same computation is still available.
detail: Available-expression analysis determines which expressions are still valid at each point, killing expressions whose operands are redefined.
proof: If available-expression analysis proves the operands retained their values since the earlier computation, reusing the stored result yields the same value.
consequence: The optimisation is especially effective across repeated address calculations.

title: Loop-Invariant Code Motion
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Loop-invariant code motion moves computations that depend only on loop-invariant values outside the loop, provided the move introduces no new exceptions or side effects.
short: Compute once outside the loop what would otherwise be recomputed each iteration.
detail: Safety checks ensure the hoisted instruction executes at least as often as in the original and does not change exception behaviour.
proof: An expression whose operands never change inside the loop has the same value on every iteration, so computing it once before entry yields the same results.
consequence: Hoisting is a major source of speedups in numeric and array code.

title: Register Allocation via Graph Colouring
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Register allocation can be modelled as graph colouring: vertices are live ranges and edges connect interfering ranges that cannot share a register. Colouring with k colours assigns k machine registers.
short: Interfering live ranges need different registers, like adjacent vertices need different colours.
detail: Chaitin-style allocators simplify the interference graph by removing low-degree vertices and then colour greedily during spill-recovery.
proof: Two variables simultaneously live cannot share a register without destroying a value, so a proper colouring of the interference graph is a valid allocation.
consequence: Colouring gives a principled framework for one of the backend's most important tasks.

title: Spilling and Rematerialisation in Register Allocation
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: When a live range cannot be coloured with the available registers, the allocator spills it to memory. Rematerialisation recomputes a cheap value on demand instead of storing and reloading it.
short: Either save a value to memory or recreate it cheaply when needed.
detail: Spill code inserts loads and stores at defined points; rematerialisation is preferred for constants and simple address computations.
proof: Removing a spilled vertex lowers interference degree until colouring succeeds; if a value is cheap to recompute from live operands, recomputation is a correct alternative to storage.
consequence: Good spill choices often matter more than the colouring heuristic itself.

title: Instruction Scheduling for Pipeline Latency
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Instruction scheduling reorders independent instructions to fill delay slots created by long-latency operations while preserving data dependences and observable ordering.
latex: load\ r1;\ use\ r1\Rightarrow\text{insert independent work}
short: Do useful work while waiting for a slow operation to finish.
detail: List scheduling builds a dependence graph and repeatedly picks a ready instruction with highest priority. Speculative scheduling must respect exception semantics.
proof: Reordering instructions with no dependence between them leaves data flow unchanged while allowing the processor to overlap latency with other work.
consequence: Scheduling is essential to exploit superscalar and pipelined processors.

title: Static Linking and Relocation
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A static linker resolves symbolic references among object files, combines their sections, and applies relocations so that addresses refer to the final program layout.
short: The linker patches placeholder addresses once the final layout is known.
detail: Object files contain symbol tables and relocation entries describing where patches are needed. Static linking produces a self-contained executable.
proof: Each object file lists placeholder locations and symbolic targets; after assigning section addresses the linker resolves symbols and rewrites each placeholder with the final value.
consequence: Relocation is the mechanism that makes separately compiled modules combinable.

title: Just-in-Time Compilation and Warm-Up
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A just-in-time compiler translates bytecode to native machine code at run time, typically for frequently executed methods. Warm-up is the early period when interpretation dominates before hot code is compiled.
short: Compile at run time only the code that proves worth compiling.
detail: JIT compilers use execution profiles to guide optimisation, which can produce better code than ahead-of-time compilation for dynamic languages.
proof: Monitoring identifies hot methods; compiling them with profile information produces native code whose speed justifies the compilation cost.
consequence: JIT compilation combines portability with strong steady-state performance.

title: Tiered Compilation in HotSpot JVM
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Tiered compilation runs code first in an interpreter, then in a lightly optimising compiler, and finally in an aggressively optimising compiler as invocation counts grow.
short: Spend compilation effort only on code that proves hot.
detail: Lower tiers produce code quickly and gather profiles; higher tiers use those profiles for expensive optimisations such as inlining and speculative type specialisation.
