proof: The lower tiers have low compilation cost and supply profile data, so delaying expensive optimisation until a method is hot avoids wasting effort on cold code.
consequence: Tiered execution improves both startup time and peak throughput.

title: Deoptimisation and Bailout in JIT
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A JIT compiler can deoptimise specialised native code back to bytecode when an assumed condition fails, such as an unexpected object type. Bailout preserves language semantics despite speculative optimisation.
short: Guard the optimistic assumptions and fall back when they break.
detail: Deoptimisation reconstructs interpreter frames from the compiled state, including inlined frames, which requires precise metadata.
proof: Guards detect violated assumptions and transfer control to an unoptimised representation whose execution reproduces the specified behaviour.
consequence: Speculative optimisation can be aggressive without sacrificing correctness.

title: Escape Analysis and Scalar Replacement
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Escape analysis determines whether an allocated object can be referenced outside its creating method or thread. Non-escaping objects may be scalar-replaced, keeping their fields in registers rather than on the heap.
short: Avoid allocating objects that never leave the local scope.
detail: Escape information also enables lock elision because thread-local objects need no synchronisation.
proof: If no reference to the object survives the analysis scope, substituting its component values is observationally equivalent and removes allocation and collection work.
consequence: Escape analysis reduces garbage-collector pressure and synchronisation cost.

title: Inline Expansion in Compilers
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Inlining replaces a function call with the callee's body, removing call overhead and exposing optimisations across the former boundary. Excessive inlining can increase code size and hurt instruction-cache locality.
short: Substitute a call by its body to expose more optimisation opportunities.
detail: Inlining decisions use call frequency, callee size, and profile data. Recursive functions need special handling or size cutoffs.
proof: Binding parameters to argument values and substituting the callee's body implements the same computation, so the transformed program is semantically equivalent.
consequence: Inlining is often the optimisation that enables many others.

title: GC Roots and Reachability
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A tracing garbage collector treats stack variables, registers, globals, and runtime internals as roots and reclaims objects unreachable from them. Garbage is defined by reachability, not by reference count.
short: Anything the program can no longer reach can be reclaimed.
detail: Precise collectors need accurate stack maps identifying which slots hold references; missing a root would incorrectly reclaim a live object.
proof: An object unreachable from any root can never be accessed by the program again, so reclaiming its storage is safe.
consequence: Root accuracy is a correctness requirement for automatic memory management.

title: Tri-Colour Marking Invariant
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Incremental tracing collectors colour objects white, grey, and black. The tri-colour invariant forbids a black object from pointing directly to a white object, ensuring all reachable objects are eventually discovered.
short: Maintain a grey frontier so tracing cannot lose a reachable object.
detail: Write barriers re-grey a source or shade a target when a black-to-white reference is created. The invariant is broken only momentarily inside barrier code.
proof: Any white object reachable from a root must be reached through a grey frontier; if a black-to-white edge appears, a barrier restores the invariant by greying one endpoint.
consequence: The invariant is the correctness foundation of concurrent and incremental collectors.

title: Stop-the-World versus Incremental Collection
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: Stop-the-world collectors pause application threads while tracing, which is simple but can cause long pauses. Incremental and concurrent collectors interleave tracing with execution and use barriers to stay correct.
short: Shorter pauses are bought with more sophisticated coordination.
detail: Concurrent collectors must handle the heap graph changing during marking and usually stop briefly for final root rescanning.
proof: Pausing prevents mutation during tracing; allowing mutation requires barriers that record changes so the collector does not overlook newly reachable objects.
consequence: Pause-time goals drive the choice of collector design.

title: Write Barriers and Remembered Sets
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A generational collector records cross-generation references in a remembered set using write barriers on pointer updates. Minor collections then scan roots plus the remembered set instead of the whole heap.
short: Remember the old-to-young pointers so young collections stay cheap.
detail: Card marking divides the old generation into cards and flags a card when a pointer inside it is updated. Remembered sets must be maintained even during concurrent phases.
proof: Old-to-young pointers are the only non-root way a young object can be reachable after a minor collection, so recording them at write time suffices to find all live young objects.
consequence: Write barriers are a small per-write cost that makes generational collection practical.

title: Conservative Garbage Collection
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A conservative collector scans memory without precise type information and treats any bit pattern that could be a pointer as a possible reference. It is safe without accurate pointer maps but may retain unreachable objects.
short: Better to keep a dead object than to reclaim a live one.
detail: Conservative collection works with languages such as C where pointer locations cannot always be identified. Interior pointers can force an entire object to be retained.
proof: Treating every plausible pointer as genuine can only retain extra objects, never reclaim a reachable one, so the collector is safe though imprecise.
consequence: Conservative collectors trade memory efficiency for language compatibility.

title: Bytecode Verification in the JVM
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: The JVM verifier checks that untrusted bytecode respects type and stack discipline before execution, preventing forged pointers and stack corruption. Verification is a static dataflow analysis over the instruction graph.
short: Prove type safety of bytecode before allowing it to run.
detail: Verification tracks operand-stack and local-variable types at every instruction and checks that all control-flow paths agree at merge points.
proof: Abstract interpretation of types along every control-flow path shows each instruction receives values of expected types, so malformed code is rejected before execution.
consequence: Verification is a key part of the JVM sandboxing model.

title: Garbage Collection Safepoints
subject: Compilers & Runtime Systems
statement: A safepoint is a program location where the runtime can stop all threads to inspect their roots safely. Precise collectors require threads to reach safepoints before tracing begins.
short: Stop threads only where their reference locations are known.
detail: The compiler emits safepoint polls at loop backedges and call sites. Stack maps describe which registers and stack slots contain references at each safepoint.
proof: At a safepoint the runtime knows exactly which locations hold references, giving a consistent root set; arbitrary stopping points would make root discovery unreliable.
consequence: Safepoint placement balances pause latency against poll overhead.

title: Unit Tests and Coverage Criteria
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Unit tests exercise individual program units in isolation. Coverage criteria such as statement, branch, and path coverage measure which parts of the code a test suite actually executes.
short: Coverage measures how much of the code a test suite has touched.
detail: Branch coverage is stronger than statement coverage, and path coverage is stronger still but rarely exhaustive. High coverage does not guarantee the absence of bugs.
proof: Instrumenting code records which statements or branches execute, and the ratio of executed items to total items defines the corresponding coverage metric.
consequence: Coverage gives an objective, if incomplete, measure of test-suite breadth.

title: Mutation Testing Measures Test Suite Strength
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Mutation testing creates small syntactic variants of a program and checks whether a test suite kills them by failing. A high mutation score indicates a suite sensitive to fault-like changes.
short: A test suite is strong if it notices deliberate small faults.
detail: Equivalent mutants produce the same behaviour as the original and are usually excluded. Mutation testing is computationally expensive because each mutant requires a full test run.
proof: Each mutant differs by one fault-like change; if no test distinguishes it from the original, that class of defect is undetected, so survival exposes a weakness.
consequence: Mutation scores often correlate better with defect detection than statement coverage.

title: Property-Based Testing with Generated Inputs
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Property-based testing generates many inputs and checks that a stated invariant holds for each. Shrinking reduces a failing input to a small, informative counterexample.
short: State universal properties and let the machine search for counterexamples.
detail: Generators encode the input domain, and shrinking repeatedly simplifies a failing value while preserving the failure.
proof: Generated sampling explores many inputs beyond handwritten cases; stepwise shrinking removes parts of a failing input while the property still fails, yielding a minimal witness.
consequence: Property-based testing finds edge cases that example-based tests often miss.

title: Coverage-Guided Fuzzing
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Coverage-guided fuzzing mutates seed inputs, keeps mutants that reach new code coverage, and repeats, using coverage as a search heuristic.
short: Grow a corpus of inputs that explores more of the program.
detail: Instrumentation records edge coverage, and sanitizers detect memory-safety violations during execution.
proof: Retaining inputs that expand coverage focuses search on unexplored regions, and mutation explores variations of promising seeds.
consequence: Fuzzing has discovered large numbers of real security vulnerabilities.

title: Regression Testing and Test Oracles
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Regression testing reruns existing tests after changes to detect newly introduced defects. A test oracle determines whether an execution's outcome is correct.
short: Reuse past expectations to catch behavioural changes.
detail: Oracles may be explicit expected values, reference implementations, or invariants. The oracle problem refers to cases where correctness is hard to specify.
proof: Storing expected outcomes from a trusted baseline allows later executions to be compared, so a behavioural change is detected as a regression.
consequence: Regression suites are the main defence against breaking working software.

title: Integration Testing versus System Testing
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Integration testing checks that modules interact correctly, while system testing checks the complete product against its specification. Integration tests target interfaces; system tests target end-to-end behaviour.
short: First check that pieces fit, then check the assembled product.
detail: Common integration strategies include bottom-up, top-down, and sandwich approaches using stubs and drivers.
proof: Combining modules exposes interface mismatches invisible to unit tests, while exercising the assembled system validates requirements that emerge only from the whole.
consequence: The two levels catch disjoint classes of defects.

title: Continuous Integration and Automated Builds
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Continuous integration merges changes frequently into a shared branch and automatically builds and tests each integration, detecting conflicts and regressions early.
short: Integrate often and let automation check every merge.
detail: Fast feedback encourages small changes and makes failures easy to localise to a recent commit.
proof: Building and testing on every merge shortens the interval between introducing and detecting a defect, which reduces the cost of diagnosing it.
consequence: Continuous integration is a foundation of modern collaborative development.

title: Static versus Dynamic Type Checking
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Static type checking rejects ill-typed programs before execution, while dynamic checking detects type errors during execution. Static checking catches errors earlier but can reject safe programs that a dynamic language accepts.
short: Prove safety ahead of time or check it while running.
detail: Gradual typing combines both by allowing typed and untyped code to interoperate with casts at boundaries.
proof: A static type system proves a property for all executions by construction, while dynamic checks inspect operations at run time and only report errors on paths actually taken.
consequence: The choice affects error detection timing, flexibility, and runtime overhead.

title: Hindley-Milner Type Inference
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Hindley–Milner type inference assigns principal types to expressions in a typed lambda calculus with let-polymorphism without annotations. Algorithm W computes the most general type scheme by unification.
short: Unification discovers the most general type automatically.
detail: The principal type property means every other valid typing is an instance of the inferred one.
proof: Generating fresh type variables and unifying constraints from applications yields the most general unifier, which is the principal type scheme.
consequence: ML and Haskell families combine strong static typing with little annotation burden.

title: Exhaustiveness Checking for Algebraic Data Types
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Exhaustiveness checking verifies that a pattern match covers every constructor of an algebraic data type. A non-exhaustive match can fail at run time, so compilers warn or reject such code.
short: Ensure every possible value is handled by some pattern.
detail: Nested patterns and guards complicate coverage checking; some compilers use binary decision diagrams to decide exhaustiveness.
proof: Each pattern covers a subset of constructor combinations, and comparing their union with the full constructor set detects missing cases.
consequence: Exhaustiveness makes refactoring data types safer because missing cases are reported at compile time.

title: Weakest Precondition Calculus
subject: Software Engineering
statement: The weakest precondition of a program and a postcondition is the weakest assertion guaranteeing that postcondition after execution. It is computed backwards through assignments, sequences, and conditionals.
short: Work backwards from the desired postcondition to what must hold before.
detail: For conditionals the weakest precondition is a conjunction guarded by the branch conditions; loops require loop invariants or least fixed points.
proof: Substituting e for x in Q is exactly the condition on the pre-state making Q true after the assignment; composition follows by backward propagation.
consequence: Weakest preconditions are the basis of deductive program verification tools.

title: Design by Contract
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Design by contract specifies preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants that cooperating components must satisfy. Violations identify which side of a module boundary broke the agreement.
short: Document the obligations and guarantees of every component.
detail: Eiffel integrates contracts into the language; other systems use annotations or assertion libraries.
proof: Checking preconditions at entry and postconditions and invariants at exit localises responsibility to caller or callee.
consequence: Contracts make module interfaces more precise and debugging more direct.

title: Software Refactoring Preserves Behaviour
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Refactoring restructures code without changing externally observable behaviour. Tests serve as a safety net verifying behaviour preservation across the transformation.
short: Change the structure, not the behaviour.
detail: Typical refactorings include extract method, rename variable, and replace conditional with polymorphism.
proof: Each refactoring is a behaviour-preserving transformation, and the test suite checks that observable outputs remain unchanged after applying it.
consequence: Refactoring keeps designs clean without introducing new functionality.

title: Coupling and Cohesion in Module Design
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Cohesion measures how closely related the responsibilities inside a module are, while coupling measures the strength of dependencies between modules. Good designs favour high cohesion and low coupling.
short: Keep related code together and dependencies few.
detail: Highly cohesive modules change for one reason; loosely coupled modules limit the propagation of changes across the system.
proof: A module with a single focused responsibility has fewer reasons to change, and weak dependencies reduce the number of other modules affected by a change.
consequence: These principles guide decomposition into maintainable components.

title: Semantic Versioning Rules
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Semantic versioning uses major.minor.patch numbers: a major increment signals incompatible API changes, a minor increment adds backward-compatible functionality, and a patch increment makes backward-compatible fixes.
short: Version numbers encode the compatibility impact of a release.
detail: Pre-release identifiers and build metadata extend the basic format. Consumers can express dependency constraints using these rules.
proof: The specification defines each component's meaning, so comparing two versions determines whether an upgrade should preserve existing clients.
consequence: Semantic versioning makes dependency management predictable.

title: Technical Debt Metaphor
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Technical debt describes the future maintenance cost of choosing a quick, limited solution over a more robust one. Like financial debt it accumulates interest when deferred work makes later changes harder.
short: A quick fix today can make every future change more expensive.
detail: Debt may be deliberate and beneficial when a short-term goal justifies it, but it becomes harmful when it is invisible or never repaid.
proof: A shortcut leaves code harder to understand or extend, so subsequent changes require more effort than they would in a clean design.
consequence: Making debt visible helps teams schedule remediation.

title: Cyclomatic Complexity of Control Flow
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Cyclomatic complexity of a control-flow graph is E minus N plus twice the number of connected components. It bounds the number of linearly independent execution paths and is used as a code complexity metric.
short: Count independent paths as a measure of testing difficulty.
detail: For a single connected component the formula reduces to E minus N plus two. High cyclomatic complexity correlates with harder-to-test code.
proof: The cyclomatic number of a graph counts independent cycles, which for a single-entry single-exit flow graph equals the maximum number of independent execution paths.
consequence: The metric is widely used to flag functions that need more testing or refactoring.

title: Needham-Schroeder Protocol and Replay
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The original Needham–Schroeder symmetric-key protocol is vulnerable to replay: if an old session key is recovered, an attacker can replay a recorded message and convince a principal to accept that key.
short: A valid old message can be reused when freshness is not tied to a new nonce.
detail: The Lowe attack on the public-key variant similarly exploits a missing identity check in the response message.
proof: The replayed message carries no nonce freshly generated by the receiving principal in the current run, so it is accepted as evidence of a new session key.
consequence: The attack established that freshness mechanisms are indispensable in authentication protocols.

title: Kerberos Ticket-Based Authentication
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Kerberos authenticates clients to services using tickets issued by a trusted key distribution centre. A ticket contains a session key and client identity encrypted for the service, so the client never sends its password.
short: A trusted third party issues encrypted tickets that prove identity.
detail: The ticket-granting ticket lets a client obtain service tickets without re-entering its password; authenticators with timestamps prevent replay.
proof: Only the intended service can decrypt its ticket, and the client proves knowledge of the enclosed session key with a fresh authenticator, giving mutual authentication.
consequence: Kerberos underpins single sign-on in many enterprise environments.

title: TLS Handshake and Certificate Chain
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The TLS handshake negotiates cryptographic parameters, authenticates the server through a certificate chain to a trusted root, and derives a shared session key. Subsequent records use authenticated encryption.
short: Negotiate, authenticate, derive keys, then protect traffic.
detail: Certificate revocation checking and hostname verification are essential parts of authentication in practice.
proof: Signatures chain from a trusted root through intermediates to the server's certificate, and an ephemeral key exchange produces a session key known only to the endpoints.
consequence: TLS is the foundation of confidentiality and integrity on the web.

title: Man-in-the-Middle Attack on Unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Unauthenticated Diffie–Hellman is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack: an attacker creates one shared secret with each party and relays traffic, which neither party can detect.
short: Secret sharing without authentication gives no assurance about who the peer is.
detail: Digital signatures or certificates on the exchanged public values authenticate the parties and prevent the attack.
proof: Each endpoint accepts the attacker's public value as coming from the other party, so the attacker shares a key with each and can decrypt and re-encrypt relayed messages.
consequence: Authentication is a necessary companion to key agreement.

title: Perfect Forward Secrecy with Ephemeral Keys
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Perfect forward secrecy ensures that compromising a long-term private key does not reveal past session keys. It is achieved by generating fresh ephemeral keys per session and discarding them afterwards.
short: Past sessions stay secret even if today's long-term key leaks.
detail: TLS 1.3 requires ephemeral key exchange for this reason; static RSA key transport does not provide forward secrecy.
proof: Each session key depends on ephemeral exponents that are no longer stored, so later knowledge of the long-term signing key cannot reconstruct them.
consequence: Forward secrecy limits the damage of delayed key compromise.

title: Challenge-Response Authentication
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Challenge–response authentication proves knowledge of a secret by requiring a correct reply to a fresh random challenge. Freshness prevents an eavesdropper from replaying a previously recorded response.
short: A new random question makes old answers useless.
detail: The function may be a keyed hash, encryption, or digital signature depending on the setting.
proof: A freshly generated challenge makes the probability that a recorded response matches negligible, so a valid reply demonstrates current knowledge of the secret.
consequence: Challenge–response is a core pattern in authentication protocols.

title: Nonces Prevent Replay Attacks
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: A nonce is a value used only once, typically generated freshly at random. Including nonces in authenticated messages lets a receiver detect replayed messages from earlier runs.
short: A fresh one-time value distinguishes this run from every earlier run.
detail: Nonces may be random numbers or counters, but they must not repeat within the relevant security context.
proof: The receiver compares the nonce with values seen in current runs; an old message carries a nonce that does not match a freshly generated one.
consequence: Nonces are a simple and widely used freshness mechanism.

title: Bell-LaPadula Confidentiality Model
subject: Formal Methods
statement: The Bell–LaPadula model enforces confidentiality using two rules: no read up, so a subject cannot read a higher classification, and no write down, so it cannot write to a lower classification.
short: Information may flow upward in sensitivity but never downward.
detail: The simple security property and the star property are state invariants of the model, applied to subjects and objects with security levels.
proof: Forbidding reads from higher levels and writes to lower levels prevents information from reaching a subject with insufficient clearance.
consequence: The model is the classical formal basis for mandatory access control.

title: Biba Integrity Model
subject: Formal Methods
statement: The Biba integrity model is the dual of Bell–LaPadula: subjects may not read lower-integrity data and may not write to higher-integrity data, preventing contamination of trusted information.
short: Reverse the information-flow rules to protect integrity rather than secrecy.
detail: Biba uses integrity levels and can be combined with confidentiality models when both properties matter.
proof: Reversing the direction of Bell–LaPadula's flow restrictions keeps low-integrity data from influencing high-integrity objects.
consequence: Biba is the standard formal model for integrity policies.

title: Capability-Based Security
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: In capability-based security, possession of an unforgeable reference called a capability grants authority over an object. A capability combines designation and permission in one transferable token.
short: Holding the unforgeable token is the authority.
detail: Capabilities may be implemented with kernel-protected handles or unguessable cryptographic tokens, and they support fine-grained delegation.
proof: Because capabilities cannot be forged or guessed without being granted, only a holder can name and access the object with the encoded rights.
consequence: Capability systems avoid ambient authority and make least privilege easier to enforce.

title: Access Control Lists versus Capabilities
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Access control lists attach a list of permitted principals to each object, whereas capabilities attach permissions to the reference a principal holds. The two are dual in where authority is stored.
short: ACLs ask who may access an object; capabilities ask what the bearer may do.
detail: Delegation is easy with capabilities but awkward with ACLs, while revocation is often easier with ACLs.
proof: An ACL is consulted at the object on each access, while a capability is presented with the request; passing a capability simply transfers the reference.
consequence: The distinction shapes the design of operating systems and distributed authorization systems.

title: Principle of Least Privilege
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The principle of least privilege grants each component only the permissions it needs for its legitimate task and no more. It limits damage from accidents and compromised components.
short: Give exactly the permissions required, nothing more.
detail: It applies to users, processes, and services, and is implemented through roles, sandboxing, and scoped tokens.
proof: Restricting rights reduces the set of actions available to a faulty or compromised component, bounding the harm it can cause.
consequence: Least privilege is a baseline requirement in security engineering.

title: Defence in Depth
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Defence in depth layers independent security controls so that failure of one does not expose the system. Typical layers include firewalls, authentication, encryption, logging, and input validation.
short: Several independent barriers are safer than one perfect one.
detail: The principle acknowledges that individual controls fail and aims to slow or detect an attacker rather than rely on a single boundary.
proof: An attacker must defeat several independent controls, so overall compromise probability is lower than with a single control.
consequence: Layered defences reduce risk from both known and unknown vulnerabilities.

title: Password Salting against Rainbow Tables
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Salting stores a unique random value with each password hash so identical passwords produce different hashes. Precomputed rainbow tables become ineffective because each salt requires its own table.
short: A per-account random value defeats precomputed password tables.
detail: Salts need not be secret, but they must be unique and generated with sufficient randomness.
proof: Including a different salt per account in the hash input means a precomputed chain for one salt cannot be reused for another account.
consequence: Salting is mandatory in any password storage scheme.

title: Key Stretching with bcrypt
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Key stretching applies a deliberately expensive iterative computation to a password before storing the derived value. Schemes such as bcrypt slow offline guessing while keeping legitimate logins tolerable.
short: Make every password guess expensive.
detail: The work factor can be increased over time as hardware gets faster. Memory-hard schemes such as Argon2 also limit GPU and ASIC advantages.
proof: An attacker must repeat the full work factor for every guess, so raising the iteration count increases attack cost linearly while each legitimate login pays it only once.
consequence: Key stretching substantially raises the cost of offline cracking.

title: Multifactor Authentication Factors
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Multifactor authentication requires credentials from at least two distinct categories: something the user knows, something the user has, and something the user is. Combining categories reduces the impact of a single stolen credential.
short: Two different kinds of evidence beat two of the same kind.
detail: A password plus a hardware token is stronger than two passwords because the attack surfaces differ.
proof: Compromising one factor leaves at least one independent barrier, so an attacker must break multiple distinct mechanisms.
consequence: Multifactor authentication is recommended for high-value accounts.

title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework in which a client obtains a limited access token from an authorization server and uses it with a resource server. It delegates access without sharing the resource owner's credentials.
short: Delegate limited access using scoped, expiring tokens.
detail: Authorization code with PKCE is the recommended flow for public clients; implicit flows are deprecated.
proof: The token encodes scope and expiry, so the client acts only within the granted permissions and the resource owner's password never reaches it.
consequence: OAuth 2.0 is the dominant delegation protocol for web APIs.

title: Zero Trust Architecture
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Zero trust architecture assumes no implicit trust based on network location and requires continuous verification of identity, device state, and policy for every access request.
short: Network position is not evidence of trustworthiness.
detail: It replaces perimeter-based defences with per-request authentication, authorisation, and least-privilege access.
proof: Treating each request independently means a breached internal host gains no automatic access to other resources, limiting lateral movement.
consequence: Zero trust guides the design of modern enterprise and cloud networks.

title: Linear Temporal Logic Semantics
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Linear temporal logic extends propositional logic with operators over time along a single path: next, eventually, globally, and until. Formulas are evaluated at positions of an infinite execution trace.
short: Express properties of sequences, such as eventually reaching a goal.
detail: LTL is interpreted over linear traces, in contrast to branching-time logics such as CTL. Safety and liveness properties are naturally written in LTL.
proof: The semantics are recursive on traces: eventually holds if some future position satisfies p, globally if all positions do, and p until q if q holds at a future point with p holding before it.
consequence: LTL is the standard specification language for model checkers of reactive systems.

title: Computation Tree Logic and Branching Time
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Computation tree logic quantifies over branching futures using path quantifiers A and E combined with temporal operators. It expresses claims such as 'on all paths eventually p' or 'there exists a path where p holds until q'.
short: Branching-time logic asks whether all or some futures satisfy a temporal property.
detail: CTL differs from LTL by allowing path quantification at every temporal operator, making it suitable for state-based model checking.
proof: A formula is evaluated at a state of a transition system by considering all or some outgoing paths and applying the temporal operator along each chosen path.
consequence: CTL is the specification language of several classical model checkers.

title: Kripke Structures for Model Checking
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A Kripke structure consists of states, a transition relation between them, and a labelling of states with atomic propositions. It is the standard semantic model for temporal-logic model checking.
short: A labelled transition system gives temporal formulas a precise meaning.
detail: Paths through the structure represent possible executions, and total transition relations ensure every finite prefix has an extension.
proof: The transition relation generates all executions and the labelling determines which atomic propositions hold at each state, giving an interpretation of temporal formulas.
consequence: Model-checking algorithms compute the set of states satisfying a formula over such a structure.

title: Safety and Liveness Properties
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Safety properties state that nothing bad ever happens, while liveness properties state that something good eventually happens. Every property of infinite traces is the intersection of a safety property and a liveness property.
short: Safety is refuted by a finite prefix; liveness needs an infinite trace.
detail: Mutual exclusion is safety, while eventual progress is liveness. Deadlock freedom combines aspects of both.
proof: Safety violations occur at some finite prefix, whereas liveness violations require an infinite trace with no good event; this distinction yields the decomposition theorem for trace properties.
consequence: The distinction determines what kind of counterexample a model checker must produce.

title: State Explosion Problem in Model Checking
subject: Formal Methods
statement: The global state space of a concurrent system grows roughly as the product of its components' state counts, making explicit enumeration infeasible for large systems.
short: Composing components multiplies their state spaces.
detail: Symbolic representations, partial-order reduction, symmetry reduction, and abstraction all attack different aspects of the explosion.
proof: A global state is a tuple of component states, so the number of possible tuples is the product of component counts and is exponential in the number of components.
consequence: Coping with state explosion is the central engineering challenge of model checking.

title: Symbolic Model Checking with BDDs
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Symbolic model checking represents sets of states and transition relations with reduced ordered binary decision diagrams rather than enumerating states individually. This can compress exponentially many states into manageable graphs.
short: Represent whole state sets as Boolean functions.
detail: Reachability is computed by repeated image operations on BDDs until a fixed point is reached.
proof: A reduced ordered BDD is a canonical representation of a Boolean function; applying image and preimage operators symbolically computes reachable states without visiting each state one at a time.
consequence: BDD-based checking verified many hardware designs with enormous state spaces.

title: Bounded Model Checking with SAT
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Bounded model checking encodes the existence of a counterexample of length k as a propositional formula. A satisfying assignment gives a concrete execution trace violating the property.
short: Search for a short violating trace using a SAT solver.
detail: Increasing k gives completeness up to a bound, while induction or diameter bounds can establish absence of longer counterexamples.
proof: The formula encodes the transition relation for k steps and the negation of the property at some step, so any satisfying assignment describes a valid error trace.
consequence: Advances in SAT solving have made BMC highly effective for hardware and software.

title: Bisimulation Equivalence
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A bisimulation is a relation between states of two transition systems such that related states match each other's moves and reach related successors. Bisimilar states satisfy the same branching-time temporal formulas.
latex: R\subseteq S_1\times S_2,\quad s_1\ R\ s_2
short: Two systems are equivalent if each can mimic the other's every move.
detail: Bisimulation is finer than trace equivalence because it preserves branching structure, not merely the set of observable sequences.
proof: The back-and-forth conditions let every step from one state be matched from the related state, so modal and branching-time formulas cannot distinguish them.
consequence: Bisimulation is the standard behavioural equivalence for concurrent processes.

title: Petri Nets Model Concurrent Systems
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A Petri net is a bipartite graph of places and transitions in which tokens mark places and enabled transitions consume tokens from inputs and produce tokens on outputs. It models concurrency, synchronisation, and resource sharing.
short: Token flows describe concurrent activity and resource use.
detail: Place invariants and transition invariants support static analysis of reachability and boundedness properties.
proof: A transition fires only when its input places hold enough tokens, and the marking update records the resulting distribution, so firing sequences represent concurrent executions.
consequence: Petri nets are widely used to model protocols, workflows, and manufacturing systems.

title: DPLL and CDCL SAT Solving
subject: Formal Methods
statement: DPLL decides propositional satisfiability by branching on variables with unit propagation and pure-literal elimination. CDCL extends it by deriving conflict clauses and backjumping to the decision level responsible for the conflict.
short: Learn from conflicts so the search does not repeat mistakes.
detail: Conflict clauses are derived by resolution and often include learnt literals that guide subsequent branching heuristics.
proof: A learnt clause is implied by the original formula and excludes the failing assignment, so backjumping to the asserted level preserves completeness while avoiding repeated conflicts.
consequence: CDCL solvers power verification, planning, and many combinatorial applications.

title: Satisfiability Modulo Theories
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Satisfiability modulo theories decides satisfiability of Boolean combinations of formulas over background theories such as arithmetic, arrays, or bit vectors. SMT solvers combine a SAT solver with specialised theory solvers.
short: Boolean search paired with decision procedures for richer theories.
detail: The Nelson–Oppen combination method merges disjoint theories by exchanging equalities between shared terms.
proof: The SAT solver treats theory atoms as Boolean variables, theory solvers check consistency of candidate assignments, and returned conflicts refine the Boolean search.
consequence: SMT is the engine behind program verification, symbolic execution, and software analysis tools.

title: Widening Operators in Abstract Interpretation
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A widening operator accelerates fixed-point computation over infinite abstract domains by extrapolating increasing chains after finitely many steps. It trades precision for guaranteed convergence.
short: Force an ascending analysis to stabilise while staying sound.
detail: Narrowing can recover precision after widening by descending toward a more accurate fixed point.
proof: Widening guarantees that ascending chains stabilise; because each widened step over-approximates the concrete update, the resulting fixed point remains a sound over-approximation.
consequence: Widening makes static analysis of loops and recursive programs terminates in practice.

title: Proof-Carrying Code
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Proof-carrying code attaches a machine-checkable safety proof to a program so a consumer can validate it without trusting the producer. The proof is checked against a specified safety policy before execution.
short: Ship a proof along with the code and check it locally.
detail: The trusted computing base is reduced to a small proof checker rather than a complex compiler or verifier.
proof: The checker validates the proof in a small trusted kernel, and a valid proof establishes that the code satisfies the safety policy.
consequence: Proof-carrying code enables safe execution of untrusted software from arbitrary sources.

title: Runtime Verification with Monitors
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Runtime verification checks a property against an executing system using a monitor that observes events and issues verdicts. It is lighter than model checking but covers only the executions actually observed.
short: Check a specification against the running system's event stream.
detail: Monitors can be generated automatically from temporal logic formulas and may be online or offline.
proof: The monitor is an automaton for the property specification, so processing an observed trace determines whether a prefix violates the property or satisfies it.
consequence: Runtime verification bridges formal specification and deployed systems.

title: Temporal Logic Model Checking Algorithm
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Explicit-state temporal-logic model checking labels states with satisfied subformulas bottom-up, using set operations for Boolean connectives and fixed points for until and globally operators.
short: Compute the set of states satisfying each subformula in turn.
detail: The until operator is the least fixed point of a monotone function on state sets, while globally is a greatest fixed point.
proof: Atomic propositions give base sets, Boolean operators use set operations, and iterating the monotone until operator from the empty set yields exactly the states with a witnessing path.
consequence: The decision procedure runs in time polynomial in the model and formula size.

title: Fitts's Law of Pointing Time
subject: Computer Science
statement: Fitts's law models movement time to a target as a logarithmic function of the distance to the target divided by its width. Larger and closer targets are acquired more quickly.
short: The index of difficulty grows logarithmically with distance over width.
detail: The law applies to mouse pointing, touch input, and many motor tasks, with device-specific constants.
proof: Controlled experiments show movement time is linear in the index of difficulty log2(1+D/W) across a wide range of target sizes and distances.
consequence: Interface designers use the law to choose target sizes and place frequently used controls close at hand.

title: Hick's Law of Choice Reaction Time
subject: Computer Science
statement: Hick's law states that decision time grows logarithmically with the number of equally likely choices. Each additional option adds less time than the previous one.
short: More choices slow decisions, but with diminishing returns.
detail: The law is used to design menus and to justify progressive disclosure of rarely used options.
proof: Subjects behave approximately as if performing a binary search through the alternatives, so the expected number of decisions grows as log2 of the choice count.
consequence: Reducing simultaneous choices can speed user decisions, especially in time-critical interfaces.

title: Nielsen's Usability Heuristics
subject: Computer Science
statement: Nielsen's ten usability heuristics are broad design principles including visibility of system status, match with the real world, user control and freedom, consistency, error prevention, and flexibility.
short: A short checklist for finding usability problems in an interface.
detail: Heuristic evaluation asks inspectors to compare an interface against each principle and list violations with severity ratings.
proof: The heuristics distil recurring findings from usability practice into a compact checklist, which inspectors apply systematically to find problems cheaply.
consequence: Heuristic evaluation finds many issues early without user studies.

title: Affordances and Signifiers
subject: Computer Science
statement: An affordance is an action an object supports, while a signifier communicates where that action is available. Good interfaces make useful affordances visible through signifiers such as shape, labels, and icons.
short: Show users what can be done and where.
detail: A button's raised appearance is a signifier for clickability; a flat unlabelled region may hide an equally real affordance.
proof: Users infer possible actions from perceived properties, so signifiers make supported actions discoverable without trial and error.
consequence: Clear signifiers reduce exploration and misuse in interfaces.

title: Cognitive Load Theory for Interfaces
subject: Computer Science
statement: Cognitive load theory distinguishes intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load. Interfaces should minimise extraneous load so users can devote limited working memory to the task itself.
short: Remove mental work that does not contribute to the user's goal.
detail: Consistent layouts, clear labels, and progressive disclosure all reduce extraneous load.
proof: Working memory capacity is limited, so reducing load unrelated to the task leaves more capacity for task-relevant processing.
consequence: The theory provides a principled basis for simplifying complex interfaces.

title: Feedback and Visibility in Interactive Systems
subject: Computer Science
statement: Visibility of system status requires every action to produce timely, appropriate feedback. Without feedback users cannot tell whether an action succeeded and often repeat it unnecessarily.
short: Tell users what happened so they know where they stand.
detail: Progress indicators, confirmations, and visible state changes are common forms of feedback.
proof: Feedback closes the loop between user action and system state, letting the user update their mental model and avoid duplicate actions.
consequence: Missing feedback is one of the most common sources of user frustration.

title: WCAG Accessibility Guidelines
subject: Computer Science
statement: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines define conformance levels A, AA, and AAA for making web content accessible. They cover text alternatives, keyboard access, contrast, navigation, and error identification.
short: An international checklist for accessible web content.
detail: Meeting level AA is a common legal and organisational target for public websites.
proof: The guidelines enumerate testable success criteria grouped into levels, so conformance can be assessed systematically against a published standard.
consequence: WCAG provides a shared, measurable basis for inclusive design.

title: Mental Models and User Expectations
subject: Computer Science
statement: Users interact through mental models of how a system works. Interfaces matching those expectations reduce errors, while mismatches cause confusion even if the system is technically correct.
short: Design for the model users already have, or teach them a new one clearly.
detail: Consistent metaphors and predictable feedback help users form accurate mental models.
proof: Users predict outcomes from their mental model; when predictions match system behaviour interactions succeed, while inconsistencies force relearning.
consequence: Mental-model mismatches explain many errors that are not simple usability flaws.

title: The Graphics Rendering Equation
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: The rendering equation expresses outgoing radiance at a surface point as emitted radiance plus an integral of incoming radiance weighted by the BRDF and a cosine factor over the hemisphere.
short: Light leaving a point is emission plus reflected incoming light.
detail: It is an integral equation because incoming radiance may itself have been reflected elsewhere, giving global illumination effects.
proof: Radiance leaving a point equals emitted radiance plus the contribution of incoming radiance from every direction, with the BRDF giving the fraction scattered toward the viewer.
consequence: Most photorealistic rendering algorithms are numerical solvers for this equation.

title: Rasterisation Pipeline Stages
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: The rasterisation pipeline transforms vertices by model, view, and projection matrices, clips primitives, maps them to screen coordinates, and fills pixels with interpolated attributes before shading.
short: Geometry flows through transformations, clipping, and pixel coverage.
detail: Programmable shader stages replace fixed-function stages in modern GPUs while preserving the overall pipeline structure.
proof: Each stage applies a defined transformation to geometry or fragments, and their composition maps a 3D scene description into final pixel colours.
consequence: The pipeline structure explains both GPU hardware design and graphics APIs.

title: Ray Tracing and Recursive Rays
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Ray tracing computes pixel colours by casting rays from the camera through the image plane and finding intersections with scene geometry. Recursive secondary rays model reflection, refraction, and shadows.
short: Follow light paths from the camera to estimate each pixel's radiance.
detail: Acceleration structures such as bounding volume hierarchies reduce the cost of intersection tests, and recursion depth is usually capped.
proof: At each intersection the contribution is emitted light plus recursively evaluated light along reflected and refracted directions, approximating the rendering equation by path sampling.
consequence: Ray tracing naturally produces shadows, reflections, and global illumination effects.

title: Z-Buffer Depth Testing
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: The z-buffer algorithm stores a depth value per pixel and keeps the fragment whose depth is smallest. It resolves visibility independently for each pixel without sorting all primitives globally.
short: Keep only the nearest fragment at each pixel.
detail: Depth precision and near-plane placement affect z-fighting between close surfaces.
proof: Replacing a pixel only when the incoming fragment is closer ensures the stored colour belongs to the nearest surface along the view ray.
consequence: Depth buffering is the dominant hidden-surface method in real-time graphics.

title: Painter's Algorithm and Depth Sorting
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: The painter's algorithm draws distant primitives first so nearer ones cover them. It requires a global depth order and fails for intersecting polygons or cyclic overlap.
short: Draw back to front, but overlapping cycles have no valid order.
detail: Newell's algorithm splits polygons to handle many cyclic cases at extra cost.
proof: If every primitive is drawn after all primitives behind it, the last colour written at each pixel is that of the nearest covering primitive; cyclic overlap prevents such an order.
consequence: Depth buffering has largely superseded pure painter's ordering in interactive rendering.

title: Backface Culling by Winding Order
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Backface culling discards triangles whose projected vertex winding is opposite to the chosen front-face convention, avoiding work on surfaces facing away from the camera.
short: Triangle orientation reveals which side faces the viewer.
detail: Double-sided objects must disable culling or render both orientations explicitly.
proof: For closed objects with consistent winding, a triangle whose normal points away from the camera cannot be visible from outside, so discarding it is safe.
consequence: Culling roughly halves geometry work for typical closed meshes.

title: Phong Shading Model
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: The Phong shading model computes surface intensity from ambient, diffuse, and specular terms, interpolating normals across a polygon and evaluating lighting per pixel.
short: Ambient fill, cosine-lit diffuse, and a power-law highlight.
detail: The exponent controls highlight sharpness; Blinn–Phong uses a half vector for cheaper and often more plausible highlights.
proof: Lambert's cosine law gives the diffuse term, and raising the alignment of reflected and view directions to a power approximates a specular lobe.
consequence: Phong shading is a foundational local illumination model.

title: Gouraud Shading and Vertex Interpolation
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Gouraud shading computes lighting at polygon vertices and interpolates the resulting colours across the surface. It is cheaper than per-pixel shading but can miss narrow specular highlights.
short: Light at vertices, then blend colours across the triangle.
detail: Because highlights are sampled only at vertices, a highlight centred inside a large triangle may be invisible.
proof: Barycentric weights interpolate vertex colours linearly over the triangle, giving smooth appearance using only vertex lighting computations.
consequence: It was an early and inexpensive route to smooth-shaded surfaces.

title: Barycentric Coordinates for Triangle Interpolation
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Barycentric coordinates write a point inside a triangle as an affine combination of its vertices with nonnegative weights summing to one. They give a natural way to interpolate attributes over a triangle.
short: Weights relative to triangle vertices drive smooth attribute interpolation.
detail: The same weights interpolate colour, texture coordinates, normals, and depth during rasterisation.
proof: Solving the affine combination for a point gives unique weights for a nondegenerate triangle, and any vertex-defined attribute interpolates with those weights.
consequence: Barycentric interpolation is a core operation of rasterisers.

title: Mipmapping and Texture Minification
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Mipmaps are precomputed lower-resolution versions of a texture. The renderer selects a level whose texel density matches the pixel footprint, reducing aliasing when a texture is minified.
short: Use a smaller prefiltered texture when pixels cover many texels.
detail: Trilinear filtering blends between adjacent mip levels for smoother transitions.
proof: Averaging texels into coarser levels band-limits the texture, so sampling a level near the pixel footprint avoids high-frequency aliasing.
consequence: Mipmapping greatly improves texture quality at oblique viewing angles.

title: Bilinear Texture Interpolation
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Bilinear interpolation blends the four texels surrounding a sample location using fractional offsets along two axes. It smooths texture magnification at modest cost.
short: Average the four nearest texels weighted by distance.
detail: Nearest-neighbour sampling is cheaper but produces blocky magnified textures.
proof: Linear interpolation along one axis followed by linear interpolation along the other yields a weighted average of the four neighbouring texels.
consequence: Bilinear filtering is a standard baseline for texture sampling.

title: Shadow Mapping Algorithm
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Shadow mapping renders the scene from the light source into a depth map, then compares each fragment's depth in light space with the stored depth to decide whether it is shadowed.
short: A fragment behind the first surface seen by the light is in shadow.
detail: A bias term avoids shadow acne caused by depth precision errors; percentage-closer filtering softens shadow edges.
proof: A fragment farther from the light than the first surface recorded in the depth map lies behind an occluder and is therefore unlit by that light.
consequence: Shadow mapping is the dominant real-time shadow technique.

title: Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Screen-space ambient occlusion estimates how exposed each pixel is to ambient light by sampling nearby depth values. Darkening occluded regions approximates global illumination cheaply.
short: Nearby geometry darkens creases and contact regions.
detail: The effect is view dependent and misses occluders outside the sampled screen neighbourhood.
proof: Nearby occluding geometry reduces the visible hemisphere for ambient light, so counting unoccluded samples gives a multiplicative approximation to ambient illumination.
consequence: SSAO adds perceptual depth cues at low rendering cost.

title: Marching Cubes for Isosurfaces
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Marching cubes extracts an isosurface from a scalar field by subdividing space into cubes and triangulating the portions of each cube where the field crosses a threshold.
short: Turn a scalar volume into a polygonal surface.
detail: The eight corner signs select a configuration from a lookup table; ambiguous cases require careful disambiguation to avoid cracks.
proof: The corner values determine which edges cross the isolevel, and a fixed lookup table gives triangle connectivity consistent across neighbouring cubes.
consequence: Marching cubes is a standard method for visualising volumetric data.

title: Bresenham's Line-Drawing Algorithm
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Bresenham's line algorithm rasterises a straight line using integer arithmetic by maintaining an error term that decides when to step along the secondary axis.
short: Choose the nearest pixel at each step without floating point.
detail: The error term is updated incrementally from the line slope, making the algorithm fast enough for early graphics hardware.
proof: The error tracks the deviation between the ideal line and the selected pixel centre, so updating it incrementally selects the closest pixel in each column.
consequence: The algorithm is a classic example of efficient incremental computation.

title: Cohen-Sutherland Line Clipping
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Cohen–Sutherland line clipping assigns each endpoint a four-bit outcode describing its position relative to a rectangular viewport and uses bitwise tests to accept, reject, or clip the segment.
short: Quickly reject obviously invisible lines and clip the rest.
detail: If both endpoints share an outside region the line is discarded; if both outcodes are zero it is accepted; otherwise it is split at a boundary and retested.
proof: A shared outside bit means both endpoints lie beyond the same boundary, so the whole segment is outside; repeated bisection at boundaries converges to the visible portion.
consequence: Outcodes give a cheap early reject in 2D clipping pipelines.

title: de Casteljau's Algorithm for Bezier Curves
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: de Casteljau's algorithm evaluates a Bézier curve by repeated linear interpolation between control points. The intermediate points also split the curve into two subcurves.
short: Repeated midpoint-style interpolation evaluates and subdivides a curve.
detail: The construction is numerically stable and forms the basis of adaptive curve subdivision.
proof: Repeated convex combinations implement the Bernstein polynomial form, so the final point equals the curve value at t and the intermediate polygons describe two subcurves.
consequence: The algorithm underlies curve rendering and CAD subdivision.

title: B-Splines and NURBS
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: B-spline curves are linear combinations of control points weighted by local polynomial basis functions. NURBS extend them with rational weights, allowing exact representation of conic sections.
short: Local basis functions give flexible, stable curve and surface modelling.
detail: B-spline basis functions have local support and form a partition of unity, so moving one control point affects only a limited part of the curve.
proof: The basis functions' local support and partition of unity make the curve a local blend of control points; dividing weighted basis functions by their sum gives the rational extension.
consequence: NURBS are the standard geometry representation in computer-aided design.

title: Alpha Blending and Compositing
subject: Computer Graphics
statement: Alpha blending combines a foreground colour with a background using an opacity value: the result is alpha times foreground plus one minus alpha times background, with premultiplied or straight alpha used consistently.
short: Opacity weights the foreground and background contributions.
detail: Order matters for non-premultiplied blending with multiple transparent layers.
proof: Alpha encodes the fraction of pixel coverage by the foreground, so a convex combination of the two colours gives the observed composite.
consequence: Alpha compositing enables transparency, antialiasing, and layered image synthesis.

title: False Sharing between Cache Lines
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: False sharing occurs when threads on different cores modify distinct variables that happen to lie on the same cache line. Coherence invalidates the whole line, causing heavy traffic despite no logical sharing.
short: Coherence granularity can create contention between unrelated variables.
detail: Padding or aligning per-thread counters to cache-line boundaries removes the effect.
proof: Coherence operates at cache-line granularity, so a write by one core invalidates the line in other cores even if they access different offsets within it.
consequence: False sharing can dominate the cost of otherwise embarrassingly parallel code.

title: Memory Barriers and Fences
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Memory barriers restrict reordering of memory operations by the compiler or hardware across the barrier. Acquire and release barriers establish ordering guarantees between threads.
short: Fences constrain when memory operations may become visible to others.
detail: A full fence orders all four combinations of loads and stores, while acquire and release fences order only relevant subsets.
proof: Hardware respects the barrier's ordering constraints, so later operations cannot be observed before an acquire and earlier operations cannot be observed after a release.
consequence: Correct lock-free algorithms depend on carefully placed barriers.

title: Race Conditions and Data Races
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A data race occurs when two threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one writes, and no synchronisation orders the accesses. Racy programs typically behave nondeterministically.
short: Unordered concurrent writes make outcomes timing dependent.
detail: Some languages declare data-race-free programs as the only ones with defined semantics.
proof: Without an ordering constraint either access may occur first, so the resulting values and subsequent control flow can depend on timing.
consequence: Eliminating data races is the first step to reliable parallel programming.

title: DRF-SC Guarantee for Data-Race-Free Programs
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A data-race-free program on relaxed hardware behaves as if its memory operations were executed in a sequentially consistent order consistent with program order.
short: Race-free code can be reasoned about as if memory were sequential.
detail: The guarantee depends on hardware or language memory models satisfying the DRF-SC condition and on correct use of synchronisation.
proof: Synchronisation operations order conflicting accesses, reducing all observable interleavings to a sequentially consistent order of the remaining operations.
consequence: Programmers can use simple sequential reasoning when synchronisation is correct.

title: Branch Target Buffers
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A branch target buffer caches destination addresses and prediction bits for recent branches so the front end can fetch along the predicted path before the branch resolves.
short: Remember where branches went last time to fetch ahead.
detail: Mispredictions squash wrongly fetched instructions and refill the buffer with the correct target.
proof: Branch behaviour shows locality, so recording previous targets lets the fetch unit continue without waiting; incorrect guesses are discarded at resolution.
consequence: Target prediction is essential for keeping deep pipelines busy.

title: Speculative Execution and Reorder Buffers
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: Speculative execution lets instructions past unresolved branches run, with results held in a reorder buffer until proven correct. Misspeculated results are discarded rather than committed.
short: Execute ahead but keep results private until they are certain.
detail: Reorder buffers also support precise exceptions by committing results in program order.
proof: The reorder buffer keeps speculative values out of architectural state, so a misprediction can be handled by discarding them and restarting on the correct path.
consequence: Speculation extracts parallelism beyond basic blocks.

title: NUMA and Memory Locality
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: In non-uniform memory access systems a processor reaches its local memory faster than memory attached to other sockets. Placing threads near the data they use improves performance.
short: Memory access time depends on where the data lives.
detail: NUMA-aware allocators and schedulers try to first-touch pages on the socket that will use them.
proof: Remote accesses traverse an interconnect adding latency and consuming bandwidth, so keeping computation near its data reduces access cost.
consequence: Ignoring NUMA placement can halve the performance of memory-bound servers.

title: TLB Shootdown on Context Switch
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: When page tables change, stale translation lookaside buffer entries in other cores must be invalidated. A shootdown interrupts those cores, which flush affected translations and acknowledge completion.
short: Broadcast invalidations so no core keeps an old mapping.
detail: Frequent shootdowns are a significant cost in systems with many cores and frequent memory-map changes.
proof: Without invalidation a core could translate using an obsolete mapping; waiting for acknowledgements ensures no stale entry remains when the operation completes.
consequence: Shootdown cost grows with core count, influencing page-table design and kernel scalability.

title: IOMMU and Device Address Translation
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: An input-output memory management unit translates device-visible addresses into physical addresses and enforces access permissions. It lets devices use virtual addresses and protects memory from faulty or malicious devices.
short: An MMU for DMA-capable devices.
detail: IOMMUs also support device assignment to virtual machines by isolating each device's address space.
proof: The IOMMU applies a translation table to each DMA request and checks permissions, so devices reach only pages the operating system mapped for them.
consequence: IOMMUs enable safe direct device access and efficient virtualisation.

title: Metastability in Clock Domain Crossing
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A signal crossing between unrelated clock domains can violate setup or hold time and become metastable before settling. Synchronisers with two or more flip-flops reduce the probability of failure.
short: Give a changing signal enough time to settle before it is used.
detail: Handshake synchronisers and FIFOs handle multi-bit crossings where simple two-flop synchronisers are insufficient.
proof: Metastability resolution is probabilistic with exponential decay in settling time, so adding a synchronisation stage multiplies the mean time between failures.
consequence: Clock-domain-crossing discipline is essential for reliable digital design.

title: Brent's Theorem on Parallel Time
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: A computation with work W and critical-path length S can be scheduled on p processors in time at most W/p plus S.
short: Time is bounded by ideal work splitting plus the critical path.
detail: The bound is tight up to constants for greedy schedulers and underlies work-span analysis.
proof: A greedy scheduler keeps all but one processor busy while the critical path advances, giving the additive bound on execution time.
consequence: Span, not only total work, determines achievable speedup.

title: Message Passing Interface Collectives
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: MPI collectives such as broadcast, reduce, scatter, and allreduce coordinate communication among a group of processes. Allreduce combines values from all ranks and delivers the result to every rank.
short: Group communication operations hide the details of multi-party exchange.
detail: Tree and butterfly algorithms implement collectives with logarithmic communication steps.
proof: Combining partial reductions in a communication tree gives every rank the same associative reduction result after logarithmically many rounds.
consequence: Collectives are heavily used in scientific computing and distributed training.

title: Work-Stealing Schedulers
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: In work stealing, each processor owns a deque of ready tasks and steals from another processor's deque only when it runs out of work. The scheme balances load with mostly local operations.
short: Work locally, steal only when idle.
detail: Stealing from the opposite end of the deque reduces contention with the owner and tends to take larger subtrees.
proof: Local operations need little synchronisation, while stealing transfers work from busy to idle processors, improving balance without a central queue.
consequence: Work stealing is the standard scheduler in fork-join runtimes.

title: GPU Warp Divergence
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: A GPU executes threads of a warp in lockstep, so when they take different control-flow paths the hardware serialises the paths. Divergence can greatly reduce effective throughput.
short: Threads that disagree on a branch run in separate passes.
detail: Predication can replace short divergent branches with masked instructions to avoid serialisation.
proof: All lanes share one instruction stream, so distinct outcomes are executed in separate passes with inactive lanes masked, summing their costs.
consequence: Branch-free or branch-uniform code is important for GPU performance.

title: Coalesced GPU Memory Access
subject: Parallel Computing
statement: GPU memory is most efficient when consecutive threads access consecutive addresses, allowing requests to merge into a few wide transactions. Strided access wastes bandwidth.
short: Contiguous accesses by a warp minimise memory transactions.
detail: Array-of-structures layouts can fragment accesses, whereas structure-of-arrays layouts often coalesce them.
proof: The memory subsystem groups neighbouring addresses into one transaction, so contiguous access by a warp serves all lanes with minimal requests.
consequence: Data layout is as important as arithmetic optimisation on GPUs.

title: Load Balancing Algorithms
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Load balancing distributes work across servers or processors so no single one is overloaded. Static schemes assign work in advance, while dynamic schemes react to observed load.
short: Spread requests so that no server becomes a bottleneck.
detail: Round-robin, least-connections, and consistent hashing are common choices with different assumptions about request costs.
proof: Sending new work to the least loaded server reduces the maximum imbalance; round robin balances only when requests have similar cost.
consequence: Good balancing improves latency and resource utilisation at scale.

title: Content Delivery Networks and Edge Caching
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: A content delivery network caches content at geographically distributed edge nodes so users fetch it from a nearby server. This reduces latency and origin bandwidth.
short: Move content close to users to shorten network paths.
detail: Cache invalidation and request routing determine how much traffic the origin still sees.
proof: Serving from a nearby cache shortens the network path and avoids repeated long-haul transfers when the cached copy is fresh.
consequence: CDNs are essential to the performance and reliability of large web services.

title: Serverless Cold Starts
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Serverless platforms start function instances on demand. A cold start is the extra latency of provisioning and initialising a new instance before handling the first request.
short: On-demand execution pays startup cost on the first call.
detail: Keeping instances warm, shrinking packages, and pre-initialising runtimes reduce cold-start latency.
proof: With no warm instance available the platform must load code and initialise the runtime, adding startup time to that request.
consequence: Cold starts matter for latency-sensitive serverless applications.

title: Microservices and Service Decomposition
subject: Software Engineering
statement: Microservices architecture splits an application into small independently deployable services with well-defined interfaces and separate data ownership. It increases autonomy but adds network and operational complexity.
short: Independent services trade local simplicity for distributed complexity.
detail: Each service can be scaled and released independently, but failures and latency become distributed concerns.
proof: Independent deployment follows from separate code and data ownership, while interactions become remote calls that need versioning, discovery, and failure handling.
consequence: The architecture suits large organisations more than small applications.

title: Circuit Breaker Pattern
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: A circuit breaker monitors calls to a remote service and stops sending requests when failures pass a threshold, later probing for recovery. It prevents cascading failures and wasted retries.
short: Stop calling a failing dependency until it recovers.
detail: Fallback responses and timeouts complement the breaker to keep the caller responsive.
proof: Blocking calls while a dependency is failing lets the caller degrade gracefully and gives the dependency time to recover before traffic resumes.
consequence: Circuit breakers improve resilience of microservice architectures.

title: Idempotency in Distributed APIs
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether applied once or several times. Idempotency keys let clients retry requests safely after ambiguous failures.
short: Retries must not duplicate the side effects of a request.
detail: Recording processed keys with their responses gives the same result on replay of a request.
proof: A unique key plus a record of processed requests maps repeated calls to the original result, so a timeout can be retried without double processing.
consequence: Idempotency is essential for reliable APIs over unreliable networks.

title: Container Orchestration with Kubernetes
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Kubernetes schedules containerised workloads on a cluster, maintains a desired number of replicas, and provides service discovery, rolling updates, and self-healing.
short: Controllers continuously drive observed state toward desired state.
detail: Declarative configuration lets operators specify intent rather than imperative steps.
proof: Controllers compare desired and observed state and take actions to close the gap, so failed containers are replaced automatically.
consequence: Orchestration makes large container deployments manageable.

title: Elastic Auto-Scaling
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Elastic auto-scaling adjusts allocated resources to observed demand, adding capacity during spikes and removing it afterwards to control cost.
short: Match resource supply to demand dynamically.
detail: Scaling policies use metrics such as CPU use, request rate, or queue depth and must account for startup delay.
proof: Monitoring drives replica-count changes that move capacity toward the level needed for the observed load target.
consequence: Elasticity is a defining economic advantage of cloud computing.

title: Distributed Tracing and Observability
subject: Distributed Systems
statement: Distributed tracing records a request's path across services as spans carrying timing and causal relationships. It helps diagnose latency and failures in microservice systems.
short: Follow one request across every service it touches.
detail: Trace context propagation, sampling, and aggregation are needed to keep overhead manageable.
proof: Propagating a trace identifier through service calls lets spans be assembled into a causal tree, revealing where time was spent across boundaries.
consequence: Tracing is a core observability tool for production distributed systems.

title: The Mars Pathfinder Priority Inversion Incident
subject: Operating Systems
statement: The 1997 Mars Pathfinder mission suffered repeated system resets caused by priority inversion between a high-priority communications task and a low-priority task holding a mutex.
short: A textbook synchronisation pitfall once threatened a planetary landing.
detail: A medium-priority task preempted the mutex holder while the high-priority task waited, so the reset watchdog fired. Enabling priority inheritance eliminated the resets.
proof: Flight software traces showed the high-priority task blocked on a lock held by a preempted low-priority task; once the holder inherited the higher priority it finished quickly and the blocking disappeared.
consequence: The incident made priority inheritance a standard consideration in real-time system design.

title: A Database Index Can Make a Query Slower
subject: Database Systems
statement: Adding an index can slow a query when its predicate matches many rows, because random row fetches through the index can cost more than a sequential scan of the table.
short: More indexing is not always faster indexing.
detail: Optimizers use selectivity estimates to decide between an index plan and a scan; stale statistics can make the wrong choice.
proof: A scan reads pages sequentially, whereas an index plan pays an index descent and often one random access per matching row, so a large match set makes the index plan more expensive.
consequence: Index design must follow workload and selectivity rather than the assumption that indexes always help.

title: The High Cost of a Branch Misprediction
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: On a deeply pipelined processor a single branch misprediction can waste more than a dozen cycles, because every younger speculative instruction must be squashed and fetched again from the correct path.
short: One wrong guess can throw away a pipeline full of work.
detail: Branch predictors therefore aim for very high accuracy, and compilers arrange likely paths to be the fall-through path.
proof: When a branch resolves incorrectly the front end discards the speculative instructions and restarts from the resolved target, paying refill and pipeline latency before useful work resumes.
consequence: Misprediction penalties explain why branch prediction is a first-order performance concern.

title: Cache Misses Can Cost More Than Arithmetic
subject: Computer Architecture
statement: A main-memory cache miss can stall a core for hundreds of cycles, far longer than the arithmetic it feeds, so data movement rather than computation dominates many kernels.
short: Moving data can be more expensive than operating on it.
detail: The roofline model captures this by comparing attainable arithmetic throughput with memory bandwidth and operational intensity.
proof: Measured memory latencies exceed single-cycle arithmetic latencies by orders of magnitude, and the roofline bound shows when bandwidth rather than compute limits performance.
consequence: Improving locality often yields larger speedups than reducing instruction counts.

title: Little's Law for Queueing Systems
subject: Operating Systems
statement: In a stable queueing system the long-run average number of items in the system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time an item spends there.
short: Occupancy equals arrival rate times average residence time.
detail: The identity requires no assumptions about the arrival distribution or service discipline beyond stability and the existence of the averages.
proof: Over a long interval the total time spent by all items equals the area under the occupancy curve, and dividing both sides by the interval length gives L equals lambda times W.
consequence: Little's law relates latency, throughput, and concurrency in servers, networks, and operating-system queues.
